item.title: Adobe Substance 3D
item.description:
Substance 3D Painter lets artists paint directly on a model with layers, masks, and smart materials that react to the shape underneath. Designer builds procedural materials from node graphs, so one material can produce many variations. Sampler turns photos and scans into tileable materials, and AI features help with that conversion.

Game studios, film teams, and product designers use it to texture assets, then export to engines such as Unreal and Unity or to renderers like Arnold. PBR output is the default, so materials look consistent across tools.

item.title: Agisoft Metashape
item.description:
Users load images from cameras or drones, align them, and generate dense geometry and textures. Archaeologists use it to document sites and artifacts, and surveyors use it for mapping. It can classify points and measure volumes.

Standard and professional editions differ in georeferencing and processing features. Good results depend on photo overlap and lighting.

Pix4D and RealityCapture are alternatives. Metashape suits archaeologists, surveyors, and conservators.

item.title: AnyLogic
item.description:
Models can use discrete-event, agent-based, or system dynamics methods, alone or combined. Users run experiments, see animations, and analyze results. Java scripting allows custom logic.

A free version exists for learning, and professional licenses are paid.

Simul8 and Arena are alternatives. AnyLogic suits industrial engineers who run simulation studies.

item.title: Autodesk Revit
item.description:
Changes made in one view update plans, sections, schedules, and quantities. Teams coordinate architecture, structure, and building systems in a shared model. Dynamo supports scripted automation, and generative design tools can test layout options.

It runs on Windows and has a steep learning curve. Large firms rely on it for coordination.

Archicad and Vectorworks are alternatives. Revit suits architects and engineers who work in BIM.

item.title: Candid
item.description:
Users search funders by location, cause, and giving history, and see past grants and contacts. A free version offers limited searches, and paid plans give full access. Candid also runs GuideStar profiles of nonprofits.

Data comes from tax filings and funder reports, so recent changes may not show.

Instrumentl is a grant discovery alternative with tracking features. Candid suits grant writers who research funders.

item.title: CephX
item.description:
CephX automates cephalometric tracing. An orthodontist uploads a lateral ceph image, the AI places the landmarks, and a full set of measurements comes back within seconds instead of the manual tracing time.

It includes many standard analyses, so a practice can pick the one it already uses. For 3D work, it can build a 2D cephalometric view from CBCT scans and includes airway analysis.

CephX is a paid service. Landmark placement still needs a clinician’s review, and the accuracy claims come mostly from the vendor. Alternatives include Owandy Ceph Analysis, Invivo, and Diagnocat. CephX suits orthodontic practices that want faster, more consistent ceph analysis.

item.title: COMSOL Multiphysics
item.description:
Users define geometry, add physics, and solve. Modules cover chemical reactions, batteries, fluid flow, and acoustics. Surrogate models can speed up repeated studies.

Licenses are costly, and the learning curve is steep for new users.

Ansys is the main alternative. COMSOL suits chemical and process engineers who need coupled models.

item.title: Dagster
item.description:
Developers define assets in Python and Dagster tracks lineage and freshness. A UI shows runs and dependencies, and tests run locally. Dagster Cloud offers a hosted service.

The open-source core is free. It differs from Airflow in structure, so teams moving over need to adjust.

Airflow and Prefect are alternatives. Dagster suits data engineers who want asset-based pipelines.

item.title: ECMWF
item.description:
Meteorologists use ECMWF forecast charts and open data to compare with other models. The centre also publishes the ERA5 reanalysis, a long record of past weather used in climate research. Its AI forecasting system adds machine learning models alongside traditional physics.

Some data is open and some is available to member states or by license.

NOAA GFS is another global model. ECMWF suits meteorologists who compare model output.

item.title: HEC-RAS
item.description:
Users build a terrain model, define channels and structures, and simulate steady or unsteady flow. Results include water surface profiles, inundation maps, and sediment transport. It works with GIS data.

The interface is technical and expects hydraulic knowledge.

MIKE and TUFLOW are commercial alternatives. HEC-RAS suits hydrologists and civil engineers.

item.title: ICC Digital Codes
item.description:
Users search codes such as the International Building Code and see local amendments where available. Premium subscriptions add tools like annotations and commentary. A free read-only view is available for many editions.

Local jurisdictions adopt and amend codes, so users should confirm what applies in their area.

UpCodes is an alternative with AI search. ICC Digital Codes suits building inspectors.

item.title: Invisalign ClinCheck
item.description:
ClinCheck is the software where Invisalign cases are planned and approved. After a scan, the system proposes a staged plan, and the doctor reviews the 3D animation and requests changes before aligners are made.

Align has added more automation over time, and the platform works with the iTero scanner and a doctor-side suite for diagnostics, patient visuals, and case tracking.

It is tied to Invisalign aligners and requires being an Invisalign provider. Alternatives for other aligner workflows include SoftSmile, uLab Systems, and 3Shape Ortho System. ClinCheck suits orthodontists already treating with Invisalign.

item.title: KeyShot
item.description:
Users drag materials onto a model, set up lighting, and see the render update live. It reads files from CAD tools such as SolidWorks and Rhino. KeyShot also includes AI-based features for texture and background creation in newer versions.

It is a paid product with subscription and perpetual options.

Blender Cycles and V-Ray are alternatives. KeyShot suits industrial designers and jewelry designers who need product renders fast.

item.title: Manhattan Associates
item.description:
Its warehouse management system directs picking, packing, and inventory placement. Order management coordinates stores, warehouses, and online orders. AI agents and optimization features help with labor planning and slotting.

It is an enterprise product, and implementations take months.

Blue Yonder and Oracle are alternatives. Manhattan Associates suits warehouse managers at large operations.

item.title: MATLAB
item.description:
It has built-in tools for matrices, signal processing, control design, and statistics. Toolboxes add machine learning, computer vision, and domain-specific functions. MATLAB can generate C code for embedded targets, and an AI assistant helps write code in newer releases.

It is standard in aerospace, automotive, and academic engineering. Licenses cost money, though many universities provide them to students, and Octave and Python are free alternatives.

MATLAB suits engineers who need validated toolboxes and a well-documented workflow.

item.title: MegaDetector
item.description:
It runs on large folders of photos and outputs boxes and confidence scores. Researchers then sort detections or pass them to species classifiers. Microsoft AI for Good started the project.

Accuracy varies with camera setup, and some manual review is still expected.

Wildlife Insights offers a web service. MegaDetector suits zoologists and wildlife biologists with large image sets.

item.title: Petrel
item.description:
Teams combine seismic, well, and production data into 3D models. Tools support geological modeling, simulation setup, and well planning. Cloud versions and AI-assisted interpretation have been added.

It is an enterprise product with custom licensing.

Seequent Leapfrog and Halliburton DecisionSpace are alternatives. Petrel suits oil and gas professionals in exploration and development.

item.title: PTV Vissim
item.description:
Users build a network, add signals and demand, and run simulations to see delays and queues. It tests design changes before they are built. It connects with other PTV tools for planning.

It is a professional license, and models need calibration with local data.

Aimsun and SUMO are alternatives. PTV Vissim suits transportation engineers.

item.title: Rhino
item.description:
Rhino models curves and surfaces with high accuracy. Grasshopper lets designers build parametric definitions with nodes, so changing a number updates a whole design. A large plug-in ecosystem covers rendering, fabrication, and analysis.

It is sold as a perpetual license rather than a subscription. The learning curve is moderate for basic modeling and steeper for Grasshopper.

SketchUp and Revit overlap in some uses. Rhino suits architects and designers who work with complex geometry.

item.title: SAS Viya
item.description:
Analysts can work in a visual interface or code in SAS, Python, or R. Model management tools track versions and monitor performance. Insurers, banks, and health organizations use it for risk and pricing models.

It is expensive and aimed at enterprises.

DataRobot, Dataiku, and Databricks are alternatives. SAS Viya suits actuaries and analysts in regulated fields.

item.title: SoftSmile
item.description:
SoftSmile makes VISION, orthodontic planning software that brings scan segmentation, diagnostics, tooth setup, and case management into one place. The AI proposes a setup and the orthodontist adjusts it.

The software finds collisions, optimizes the plan, and prepares 3D models for production, which helps practices that make their own aligners or send cases to a lab.

SoftSmile is sold to practices and labs. Time-saving figures come from the company, so test it on your own cases. Alternatives include uLab Systems, 3Shape Ortho System, and Invisalign ClinCheck. SoftSmile suits orthodontists who want AI-assisted setups with control over each step.

item.title: SolidWorks
item.description:
Users sketch features, build 3D parts, assemble them, and generate drawings. Add-ons cover simulation, sheet metal, weldments, and product data management. Recent versions add AI-assisted features for tasks like drawing creation.

It is widespread among small and mid-size manufacturers and in engineering education. It runs on Windows, and cloud versions exist.

Autodesk Fusion, Onshape, and Siemens NX are alternatives. SolidWorks suits mechanical engineers and product designers.

item.title: Tekla Structures
item.description:
Users create a model that includes connections, rebar, and bolts, then produce drawings and fabrication data. It exports to CNC machines. Collaboration works through IFC and cloud tools.

It is a paid product for specialized users.

Revit and Advance Steel are alternatives. Tekla suits structural engineers and detailers.

item.title: uLab Systems
item.description:
uLab Systems builds software for planning clear aligner treatment. Its AI proposes tooth movements from a scan, and the clinician edits the plan before approving it.

The company also supports in-office aligner production, so a practice can design and make aligners itself rather than sending every case to an outside lab.

uLab is a paid platform. The in-house approach requires printing and thermoforming equipment and some learning time. Alternatives include SoftSmile, 3Shape Ortho System, and Invisalign ClinCheck. uLab suits practices that want to control aligner design and manufacturing.

item.title: Vectorworks
item.description:
The Landmark edition adds tools for site modeling, plant libraries, and irrigation. Users can produce drawings, renderings, and schedules from the same model. It works on Windows and macOS.

It is sold by subscription or perpetual license.

AutoCAD and SketchUp are alternatives. Vectorworks suits landscape architects and designers.

item.title: Windy
item.description:
Pilots, sailors, paragliders, and outdoor guides use it to see how conditions change by altitude and hour. Layers include radar, satellite, cloud tops, and wave height. The premium plan adds extra data and removes ads.

Forecasts are model output, not guarantees, so users should compare models and check local reports when conditions are marginal.

AccuWeather and Tomorrow.io are alternatives with different focus. Windy suits anyone who needs detailed wind and weather layers.

item.title: Wolfram Mathematica
item.description:
Users work in notebooks that combine code, results, and text. The Wolfram Language has built-in functions for a huge range of math and data tasks. It connects with Wolfram Alpha knowledge and, in newer versions, with language model tools.

Licenses are paid, and student editions are cheaper.

MATLAB and SageMath are alternatives. Mathematica suits mathematicians who need symbolic power.

item.title: ZBrush
item.description:
ZBrush works with millions of polygons at once, so artists can push a model from a rough blockout to fine surface detail without switching programs. Its brush system covers everything from broad form changes to small wrinkles and scales. DynaMesh and ZRemesher help keep geometry clean while you sculpt.

Studios use it to make characters, creatures, props, and printable figures. Finished sculpts usually move into Maya, Blender, or a texturing tool for retopology, UVs, and rendering. It has a steep learning curve and an unusual interface, which new users tend to find odd at first.

item.title: Anaplan
item.description:
Anaplan lets large organizations plan in a connected way. Instead of separate spreadsheets for finance, sales, and operations, teams build models on a shared platform so a change in one area, such as a drop in demand, flows through to inventory, headcount, and budget. Its modeling engine handles large multidimensional data, and planners can create scenarios to see the effects of different decisions before committing.

AI features aim to lower the barrier to building and using models. An assistant can help create or modify model logic from natural language, forecast with machine learning, and summarize results for decision-makers. The platform integrates with ERP, CRM, and data warehouse systems to pull in actuals, and offers applications for common planning needs, such as sales territory planning and supply chain optimization.

item.title: AppFlowy
item.description:
AppFlowy is positioned as an open-source alternative to Notion. It offers documents, kanban boards, grids, calendars, and linked databases in a single workspace, and the clients are built with Flutter and Rust for desktop and mobile. You can use the cloud service or host your own server, so notes can stay on hardware you control.

Privacy and ownership are the main selling points. Data is stored locally first, the code is open for review, and teams can modify it. The AI assistant can summarize, rewrite, and answer questions about your pages, and it supports local models through tools like Ollama for people who do not want content leaving their machine.

item.title: Autodesk Maya
item.description: Maya is among the oldest and most established 3D tools in entertainment. Artists use it to model characters and environments, rig them with skeletons and controls, animate them, simulate cloth, hair, fluids, and effects, and render the result. Its animation tools, including a powerful graph editor and rigging system, are the reason it became the default in animation studios. Plug-ins and scripting in Python and MEL let studios customize it to their pipelines.

item.title: Azure AI Foundry
item.description: Foundry is where Microsoft brings together its AI development tools for businesses. A catalog lists models from OpenAI, Microsoft, Meta, Mistral, DeepSeek, and others, which you can test side by side and deploy through one set of APIs. Everything runs under Azure’s identity, networking, and compliance controls, which is what many regulated companies need before they can use generative AI. The service has gone through several names, including Azure AI Studio, so older tutorials may use different labels.

item.title: Azure AI Vision
item.description:
Azure AI Vision gives developers pretrained image analysis. The Image Analysis service can describe an image in a sentence, tag objects and scenes, detect people and objects with locations, and extract printed and handwritten text through OCR. Additional capabilities include background removal, smart cropping, and searching images by meaning, using models that understand both text and images.

Video and spatial analysis features can analyze camera feeds to count people and measure how they move through physical spaces, useful in retail and building management. Face-related features exist but are limited by a responsible AI approval process, since facial recognition has privacy and fairness concerns. Customers can also train custom models for their own image categories, and containers allow running some features on the edge.

item.title: BabyAGI
item.description:
BabyAGI arrived early in the wave of autonomous agent experiments. The original script was only a few dozen lines: given an objective, a language model creates a task list, executes the first task, stores the result in a vector database, then generates and reprioritizes new tasks based on what it learned. That simple loop was widely copied and adapted.

The project mattered because it made the idea of an AI agent easy to understand and try. It sparked many descendants and discussion about what autonomous systems could do, and developers learned from its limits, such as loops, drift, and cost. Later versions were reworked into a framework for building self-improving agents with functions stored in a database.

item.title: Baidu ERNIE
item.description:
ERNIE, which stands for Enhanced Representation through Knowledge Integration, is Baidu’s answer to ChatGPT. The consumer chatbot answers questions, writes and edits text, generates images, and handles tasks in Chinese and other languages, and it is built into Baidu’s search engine and apps. It benefits from Baidu’s knowledge graph and search data, and is a major option for Chinese-language users.

For developers and companies, Baidu offers ERNIE models through its Qianfan cloud platform, with APIs, fine-tuning, and tools for building AI applications. The company has released versions of its models with open weights, which lets developers run them independently. The models support multimodal inputs and reasoning, and are used in enterprise products, cloud services, and Baidu’s autonomous driving and other businesses.

item.title: Blender
item.description:
Blender is a complete 3D program that costs nothing. It handles modeling and sculpting, rigging and animation, physics simulation, rendering, compositing, and basic video editing in one application. It is used for animated films, game assets, product visualization, architectural renders, and motion graphics. The software is released under the GPL and developed in public by the Blender Foundation and a worldwide community, with funding from donations and corporate sponsors.

Two features define the current Blender. Cycles is a path-tracing renderer that produces photorealistic images, and EEVEE is a real-time engine for quick previews and stylized work. Geometry Nodes lets you build procedural models and effects by connecting nodes rather than editing meshes by hand, which has become popular for environments and motion design. The Grease Pencil tool allows 2D drawing and animation inside the 3D space.

item.title: Cinema 4D
item.description:
Cinema 4D is a mainstay of motion graphics. Artists use it to model objects, animate them, and render images and video for title sequences, product visuals, broadcast graphics, and advertising. It’s valued for being easier to learn than many 3D programs, with a logical interface, strong procedural tools, and reliable performance, which has made it popular with designers who need 3D without a long learning curve.

Its tools include MoGraph, a system for creating complex animations from clones and effectors, scene nodes for procedural building, simulation tools for cloth and particles, and a built-in physical renderer plus Redshift for fast, high-quality GPU rendering. It exchanges data smoothly with Adobe After Effects, Photoshop, and Illustrator, and works with game engines and other 3D programs. Maxon bundles it with other products in its Maxon One subscription.

item.title: Gemini CLI
item.description: Gemini CLI brings Gemini into the terminal as a coding and automation agent. In a project directory, you describe a task in plain language, such as explaining a codebase, fixing a failing test, or building a feature, and the agent reads files, proposes changes, runs shell commands, and iterates. It can search the web, use a context file to learn project conventions, and work with long contexts thanks to Gemini’s large context window.

item.title: Google Cloud Vision
item.description:
Google Cloud Vision is a set of pretrained image analysis features available through an API. Send an image, and it can return labels describing what it contains, detect objects and their locations, read printed and handwritten text, identify landmarks and logos, detect faces and emotions without identifying individuals, and flag explicit content with SafeSearch. It processes single images and batches, including scanned documents.

Typical uses include indexing photo libraries, extracting text from receipts and signs, moderating uploaded images, and powering search by image. Google offers related products for more specialized needs, such as Document AI for forms and Vertex AI for custom models and newer multimodal Gemini models that can describe and reason about images in more detail. Product search features help retailers match photos to catalogs.

item.title: GPT4All
item.description:
GPT4All brings language models to personal computers. After installing the app on Windows, macOS, or Linux, you choose a model from a built-in list, download it, and chat without an internet connection. Everything runs on your own CPU or GPU, so your prompts and files do not go to a remote server.

A feature called LocalDocs lets you point the app at folders of your files so the model can answer questions about them using retrieval, which makes it useful as a private research or note assistant. The project is open source and also provides libraries and bindings for developers who want to integrate local models into their own software.

item.title: Gradio
item.description: Gradio makes it easy to show a model to other people. With a few lines of Python, you wrap a function, such as one that takes an image and returns a caption, and Gradio produces a web interface with the right input and output components: text boxes, image uploaders, audio recorders, sliders, and more. Running the script gives you a local web app, and a share option creates a temporary public link, which is handy for demos and feedback.

item.title: Label Studio
item.description:
Label Studio is a flexible annotation platform. Teams use it to label data for machine learning, such as drawing boxes on images, tagging entities in text, transcribing audio, and rating language model outputs. Its configuration system lets users define custom labeling interfaces with simple markup, so one tool can serve a wide range of projects, and it runs locally or on a server.

Model-assisted labeling speeds up work. A machine learning backend can pre-label data for humans to correct, and active learning helps prioritize the most informative examples. The platform supports evaluating language models, with templates for tasks like ranking responses and checking for factual errors, which has become a common use as teams build AI applications. An API and SDK connect it with training pipelines.

item.title: LangGraph
item.description:
LangGraph models an agent as a graph. Each node is a step, such as calling a model, running a tool, or checking a condition, and edges define the flow between steps, including loops and branches. A shared state object passes information along. This explicit structure gives developers control over what the agent does and when, which makes complex agents easier to reason about than a free-running loop.

Features aimed at production use set it apart. Checkpointing saves state so a run can pause and resume, or recover from failure. Human-in-the-loop steps let an agent wait for approval before taking an action, and time-travel debugging lets developers replay and edit earlier steps. It supports streaming of intermediate results, long-term memory, and multi-agent designs, in Python and JavaScript.

item.title: o9 Solutions
item.description:
o9 targets the planning process in big supply chains. Instead of separate systems for forecasting, inventory, production, and finance, it builds one connected model of the business, called the Enterprise Knowledge Graph, so a change in demand updates the supply plan and the financial outlook. Planners can run what-if scenarios to compare options before choosing.

Machine learning forecasts demand using sales history, promotions, weather, and other signals, and the platform recommends actions such as shifting inventory or changing production. Generative AI features let planners ask questions in natural language and summarize risks. Customers include consumer goods, retail, and manufacturing companies with complex networks.

item.title: Physical Intelligence
item.description:
Physical Intelligence works on foundation models for robots. Most robots are programmed for one job, but the company aims to train a general model that can control many kinds of robots to do many tasks, such as folding laundry, clearing tables, and packing items, by learning from large amounts of robot data.

It has released research and open models, including the pi-zero family of vision-language-action models, along with code that lets other researchers try them. These models take camera images and instructions in natural language and output actions for the robot. The company collaborates with robot makers and collects data across different hardware.

item.title: Pigment
item.description:
Pigment is a modern take on planning software. Finance teams build models of their company, including headcount, revenue, and spend, in an environment that feels familiar to spreadsheet users but works with large data volumes and multiple dimensions. Plans link across departments, so a hiring plan updates the budget automatically.

It supports scenario planning, which lets teams test the impact of different assumptions side by side, and produces dashboards and reports for executives. AI agents help analyze variances, generate commentary, and build parts of models from prompts. Integrations bring in data from ERP and CRM systems and data warehouses.

item.title: RoseTTAFold
item.description:
RoseTTAFold predicts how a chain of amino acids folds into a three-dimensional protein. Knowing a protein’s shape helps scientists understand what it does and how to target it with drugs. The model was developed at the Institute for Protein Design and the University of Washington, around the same time as AlphaFold, and offered a comparable approach with a three-track neural network.

The work has grown into a family. RoseTTAFold All-Atom models complexes that include small molecules, DNA, and other components, and RFdiffusion generates new protein backbones for design tasks such as binders and enzymes. Together these tools support a shift from predicting existing proteins to creating new ones, with applications in medicine and materials.

item.title: Securiti
item.description:
Securiti addresses the problem that companies often do not know where their sensitive data lives. It scans cloud storage, databases, SaaS apps, and data pipelines, classifies personal and confidential information, and builds a map of where it sits and who can access it. This approach is known as data security posture management.

On top of that, it automates privacy and governance tasks. Teams respond to data subject requests, manage consent, run privacy assessments, and enforce policies that block risky access. For AI, Securiti helps discover models and data feeding them, apply guardrails, and meet emerging regulations, which has become a priority as companies adopt generative AI.

item.title: Superwhisper
item.description:
Superwhisper is a dictation tool. You press a shortcut, speak, and the text appears wherever your cursor is, in an email, a document, or a code editor. Because it can run speech recognition models on your own machine, nothing has to be sent to the cloud, which matters for privacy and works without an internet connection.

Modes make it more than plain transcription. A mode can clean up filler words, format the text as an email or meeting notes, translate it, or follow a custom prompt that uses a language model to rewrite what you said. It also understands context from the app you are in, and supports many languages and voice models, including cloud options for higher accuracy.

item.title: Upstart
item.description:
Upstart set out to improve how lenders decide who gets credit. Its models use many variables, including education, job history, and credit data, to predict the likelihood a borrower will repay, with the aim of approving more people at lower rates than traditional scores alone would. Borrowers apply online, often receive decisions quickly, and loans are funded by partner banks and credit unions.

The platform serves lenders as software and as a marketplace. Banks use Upstart to originate personal loans, auto loans, and home equity products, with automation that speeds approvals and reduces manual review. The company regularly tests its models for disparate impact, and has worked with regulators on fair lending, which remains a major concern for AI in credit.

item.title: Winston AI
item.description:
Winston AI is a detection tool for written content. A user pastes text or uploads a document, and the service returns a score estimating how likely it is that AI wrote it, with sentence-level highlighting. A plagiarism checker compares text against web sources, and reports can be shared as evidence.

Publishers use it to screen submissions, teachers to review student work, and agencies to check freelancers. Additional features include detection of AI-generated images and tools aimed at checking whether text has been paraphrased to evade detection. Browser extensions and an API support workflows.

item.title: AspenTech
item.description:
AspenTech sells engineering software to process industries. Chemical engineers use Aspen Plus and Aspen HYSYS to model how reactions, separations, and heat flows behave across a plant, which lets them design and test processes on screen before building them, and tune existing plants for efficiency, safety, and emissions.

The company also sells operations software. Optimization tools help plants decide how to run units to hit targets for cost and throughput, and asset performance products use machine learning on sensor data to predict equipment failures before they cause downtime. Digital twins of plant units connect design models to real operating data.

item.title: Buildertrend
item.description:
Buildertrend focuses on residential construction. Builders manage a project from estimate to completion in a single system: schedules, selections, budgets, purchase orders, daily logs, photos, and documents. Clients can log in to approve choices, view progress, and see invoices, which cuts down on phone calls.

Financial tools track costs against budgets, handle change orders, and send bills and payments. Subcontractors get access to their schedules and tasks, and mobile apps let teams update from the job site. AI features assist with tasks like summarizing communication and extracting data from documents.

item.title: Cognite
item.description:
Cognite addresses data silos in industry. A plant produces time series from sensors, maintenance records, engineering diagrams, and 3D models that live in different systems. Cognite Data Fusion links them into a graph in which a pump, its sensor readings, its work orders, and its drawings are connected, so people and applications can find everything about an asset.

That foundation supports applications. Teams build digital twins, predictive maintenance models, and dashboards, and an AI assistant helps users ask questions about assets and operations in natural language. The platform is used in oil and gas, power, and manufacturing, where downtime is costly.

item.title: Daloopa
item.description:
Daloopa serves the finance professionals who build models from public company reports. Instead of typing numbers from filings into Excel, an analyst gets a database of financial line items pulled from documents like quarterly reports and presentations, with each number linked back to its source in the original file.

Updates arrive soon after companies report, so models stay current. An Excel add-in lets analysts pull data into their own templates, and an API and integrations with AI assistants allow data to flow into other workflows. The company has focused on accuracy and traceability, since errors in financial data are costly.

item.title: Edge Impulse
item.description:
Edge Impulse brings machine learning to small devices. An engineer collects data from sensors such as accelerometers, microphones, and cameras, labels it, designs a processing pipeline, trains a model in the browser, and exports an optimized version that runs on a microcontroller or edge processor. Applications include detecting equipment faults, recognizing keywords, and spotting objects.

The platform supports a wide range of hardware and shows estimates of memory use and latency before deployment, which matters when resources are tiny. Tools help with data collection and testing, and integrations connect to major chip vendors. Qualcomm acquired the company to strengthen its edge AI offering.

item.title: Medidata
item.description:
Medidata is a major provider of clinical trial technology. Rave Electronic Data Capture collects patient data from trial sites, and other products handle randomization, imaging, patient-reported outcomes, and trial planning. Pharmaceutical companies and research organizations use the platform to run studies from start to finish.

AI and analytics help trial teams. Models flag sites with unusual data, predict enrollment problems, and help design studies using historical trial data, and the company has built synthetic control arm methods that use past patients to supplement studies. These aim to make trials faster and more efficient.

item.title: nCino
item.description:
nCino is cloud banking software. A bank uses it to manage the full lending process, from application to documents, analysis, approval, and closing, replacing paper and email chains. It covers commercial, consumer, and mortgage lending and account opening.

AI and automation reduce manual work. Models extract financial data from documents, assess credit risk, and flag items for review, and agents help with tasks like drafting credit memos. Dashboards give management visibility across the portfolio.

item.title: Physna
item.description:
Physna is a geometric search engine. Instead of searching for a part by name, a user uploads a model and the system finds others with similar shapes, even if they were named differently or came from different CAD programs. This helps find existing parts to reuse and detect duplicates.

Manufacturers use it to cut costs from redundant parts, speed up quoting, and manage large catalogs. It also supports analysis such as comparing a design with a reference and checking for intellectual property overlap.

item.title: project44
item.description:
project44 is a supply chain visibility platform. It gathers location and status data from trucks, rail, ocean, and air carriers, merges it into one view, and shows shippers where each shipment is. Predictive ETAs account for traffic, weather, and port conditions.

Alerts flag delays early, so teams can reroute or notify customers. The platform also offers tools for appointment scheduling, drayage, and analytics on carrier performance, and AI features automate routine tracking tasks and communication.

item.title: Seequent
item.description:
Seequent software helps geologists understand what lies underground. Its flagship Leapfrog creates 3D models from drill holes, geophysics, and maps, so teams can see ore bodies and structures, plan drilling, and estimate resources. Other products handle geotechnical data, groundwater, and geophysical modeling.

Mining companies, geotechnical engineers, and environmental consultants use these models for decisions. Cloud tools allow collaboration and centralized data management, and newer features apply machine learning to modeling tasks.

item.title: Shift Technology
item.description:
Shift Technology serves insurers. When a claim arrives, its models assess the likelihood of fraud, explain the red flags, and route the case, so investigators spend time on the suspicious ones while clean claims are paid quickly.

The company extends the approach to underwriting, subrogation, and customer service, and has added generative AI agents that help adjusters summarize files and handle routine tasks. Its customers include large carriers around the world.

item.title: Transkribus
item.description:
Transkribus is built for historical documents. Archivists and researchers upload scans of handwritten or old printed material, and the platform transcribes them with models that can be trained on a specific hand or period. The result is searchable text that can be corrected and exported.

It grew from European research projects and is now run by a cooperative, READ-COOP. Thousands of archives, libraries, and genealogists use it, and public models cover many languages and eras. AI search finds words across collections.

item.title: Cuey
item.description:
Cuey is a tool for comparing chatbots. From a sidebar in Chrome, you type a prompt once and it goes to services such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini that you are logged into, with the responses displayed together. A view highlights where the answers agree and differ, which is useful for fact-checking and choosing the best phrasing.

It includes a library of saved prompts and a memory feature so context can follow you from one model to another. Because it works with the chat interfaces you already use, it does not need separate API keys. The developer, Llama Valley Inc, states that prompts and responses are not stored on its servers.

item.title: Astra for Law
item.description:
Astra for Law packages OpenAI’s model for legal work. Rather than a separate model, it pairs a general model with a dedicated search index of U.S. case law, statutes, regulations, and court rules, and instructions shaped for legal analysis and drafting. The goal is research answers that are grounded in sources a lawyer can check.

Access has been limited. OpenAI offered it first to selected firms through a trusted access program, with plans to make it available to legal technology companies through the API so they can build it into their own products. Partner plugins connect it to tools used in legal practice, such as document review, practice management, and document management systems.

item.title: Enlive
item.description:
Enlive is a prompt layer. Instead of writing a long, careful prompt, a user types a brief request, and Enlive expands it with relevant context, structure, and instructions before sending it to a model. The idea is to get better answers from people who are not prompt engineers.

It works across multiple models and tracks preferences, such as tone and format, so later requests fit the user’s habits. This addresses the common experience that vague prompts return vague answers. For power users it can save the time spent rewriting prompts.

item.title: MagicShot
item.description:
MagicShot takes an all-in-one approach to generative media. Rather than paying for a different service for each task, users get a single workspace for generating images, creating video, building avatars, making product shots, and producing voiceovers, all drawing on one pool of credits.

That suits marketers and small businesses who need a bit of everything. Tools include background replacement, upscaling, style transfer, and templates for ads and social posts. Convenience comes with some compromise, as individual tools may be less advanced than specialized products.

item.title: Codex
item.description:
Codex works as a software engineering agent. A developer describes a task, such as fixing a bug or adding a feature, and Codex explores the code, makes a plan, edits files, and runs tests or linters to verify the result. It reports back with a summary of what it changed and why.

It comes in several forms. A command line tool runs on the developer’s machine, a desktop app manages multiple tasks, extensions integrate with editors like VS Code, and a cloud version in ChatGPT runs tasks in isolated sandboxes, often in parallel, and can propose pull requests on GitHub. Configuration files let teams give the agent project instructions.

item.title: DeepSeek Harness
item.description:
DeepSeek Harness is a framework for running agents that work on code. It provides the loop that lets a model plan, call tools, read and edit files, run shell commands, and report back, similar in purpose to terminal agents from other labs. Its notable design choice is that nearly every part is a plugin: the model adapter, tool registry, session log, and the agent loop itself can be replaced.

It includes presets for common setups, such as a standard coding agent with filesystem and shell tools, web search, subagents, and a planning mode, and a mode for building custom presets. Sandboxing uses the operating system’s own mechanisms to limit what the agent can touch. Although DeepSeek made it, it can connect to models from other providers.

item.title: Meta Muse Code
item.description:
Muse Code is Meta’s entry into agentic coding. A developer starts it in a project folder, describes a task, and the agent explores the code, plans changes, edits files, and runs tests, working across a repository rather than on single files. It is powered by a Meta model tuned for coding.

Meta presents it as a lower-cost option next to tools from Anthropic and OpenAI, and it runs from the command line on macOS and Linux. Features such as running sub-agents in parallel aim at larger tasks. The tool was released in beta, so expect changes.

item.title: OpenAI Daybreak
item.description:
Daybreak gives defenders access to frontier AI for security work. Approved organizations use models for tasks such as triaging incidents, analyzing malware, validating patches, and hunting for vulnerabilities, with workflows designed for security teams.

OpenAI split access into tiers. A defender tier provides frontier models without some of the safeguards that might block legitimate security prompts, and a more specialized tier provides models trained for higher-risk testing such as vulnerability research and exploit validation. Access is limited to vetted individuals and organizations.

item.title: Genspark
item.description:
Genspark started as an AI search engine and expanded into an agent workspace. A user states a goal, such as researching a market and building a presentation, and the Super Agent plans the steps, searches the web, uses tools, and produces outputs like slide decks, documents, spreadsheets, and media.

It combines several models and tools behind the scenes, and offers specialized agents for tasks like calling businesses on a user’s behalf, creating images and video, and building simple websites. Results appear in a workspace where users can review and edit them.

item.title: Google Antigravity
item.description:
Antigravity is Google’s take on an AI-first coding environment. Instead of a chat panel beside the editor, agents have direct access to the editor, the terminal, and a browser, so they can write code, run it, test the result in a browser, and report back with artifacts such as plans, screenshots, and recordings that show what they did.

Developers can run several agents in parallel and manage them from a control view. Later versions added background tasks that run on a schedule and a standalone command line tool. The environment uses Google’s Gemini models and can work with other models.

item.title: AMD ROCm
item.description:
ROCm is AMD’s answer to NVIDIA’s CUDA. It is a collection of software that lets programs use AMD graphics processors for general computing, including drivers, a compiler toolchain, math and communication libraries, and tools for debugging and profiling. Much of it is open source.

For AI work, the key piece is framework support. PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX, and others run on ROCm, and inference tools like vLLM and many model libraries have AMD builds. Developers can port CUDA code using HIP, a programming layer that resembles CUDA, and large cloud and supercomputer deployments use AMD Instinct accelerators with ROCm.

item.title: Baidu Qianfan
item.description:
Qianfan is Baidu’s cloud platform for building with large models. Companies can call Baidu’s ERNIE models and a selection of third-party and open models through a common API, then build applications such as chatbots, search over internal documents, and automated workflows. The platform covers the steps in between, including prompt engineering, fine-tuning, evaluation, and deployment.

It includes tools for agents and retrieval, with knowledge-base features that let applications answer from a company’s own data, plus plugins and workflows for connecting to business systems. Qianfan is used heavily within China, where Baidu offers local hosting and compliance with domestic regulations.

item.title: Cloudflare AI Gateway
item.description:
AI Gateway is a proxy for calls to language models. A developer points their app’s requests at a Cloudflare URL instead of the provider’s, and the gateway forwards them while recording what happens. This gives a dashboard of requests, tokens, costs, and errors across providers like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.

It adds control features. Caching returns stored answers for repeated requests to save money and time, rate limits protect budgets, and retries and fallbacks switch to another model when one fails. Logging helps debug prompts, and guardrails and key management features support security.

item.title: DeepSeek
item.description: DeepSeek is an AI research company based in China whose models are released with their weights open, so anyone can download, run, and fine-tune them. Its general-purpose models handle chat, writing, and coding, and its reasoning models work through a problem step by step before answering. What got the industry’s attention was efficiency: DeepSeek’s models perform near the best closed systems on many math and coding benchmarks while being far cheaper to train and serve. Its technical papers, which describe how it did this, are widely read by other labs.

item.title: DeepSeek Chat
item.description:
DeepSeek Chat offers consumer access to DeepSeek’s language models. Users ask questions, draft text, write code, and work through math and logic, and a mode shows the model’s step-by-step reasoning before it gives an answer. It supports uploading files and searching the web.

DeepSeek drew wide attention when its models matched strong Western systems at much lower reported training cost, and it released the model weights openly, which let others run and study them. The chat app was one of the most downloaded in many countries soon after it launched.

item.title: Mistral
item.description: Mistral is Europe’s best-known frontier AI lab. It first drew attention by releasing compact open-weight models that matched or beat larger ones, and it has continued to release models in several sizes for chat, coding, reasoning, and vision. Some are free to download under permissive licenses, while its strongest models are offered through its API and Le Chat. Developers like that it gives them the choice to run models on their own hardware.

item.title: NVIDIA NIM
item.description:
NIM, short for NVIDIA Inference Microservices, packages a model so it is easy to deploy. Each microservice includes the model, optimized inference engines such as TensorRT-LLM, and standard APIs, delivered as a container. A team can run it on a cloud, a data center, or a workstation with NVIDIA GPUs and get tuned performance.

A catalog covers language models, vision, speech, and biology models from NVIDIA and partners, with APIs compatible with common formats such as OpenAI’s. Enterprises use NIM to keep models and data inside their environment while reaching production speed.

item.title: OpenVINO
item.description:
OpenVINO helps run models efficiently on Intel hardware. A developer takes a model from PyTorch, TensorFlow, or ONNX, converts it, and optimizes it with techniques like quantization, then runs it on CPUs, integrated and discrete GPUs, and neural processing units. This makes AI practical on laptops and edge devices without a high-end graphics card.

Newer parts target generative AI, including support for language models and image generation, with a GenAI library and integration with Hugging Face. Model servers and tools support deployment in applications.

item.title: Palantir AIP
item.description:
AIP, the Artificial Intelligence Platform, is Palantir’s layer for putting language models to work on an organization’s data. It builds on Palantir’s ontology, a structured model of a company’s objects, such as orders, machines, and customers, and the actions that can be taken on them. Models can then read and act within that governed model instead of working on raw text.

Customers build agents and applications that automate tasks, answer questions, and support decisions in areas like supply chain, healthcare, defense, and manufacturing. Controls around access, logging, and human approval aim to make AI usable in sensitive settings. Palantir runs engagement programs that help customers reach production quickly.

item.title: Qwen Studio
item.description:
Qwen Studio is the consumer-facing way to use Alibaba’s Qwen models. Users chat with the assistant, search the web, upload documents and images for analysis, write code, and generate pictures and video. A mode shows the model’s reasoning for harder problems.

The Qwen family is notable for open-weight releases that developers can download and run, so Qwen Studio doubles as a showcase of what those models can do. It supports many languages, with strong coverage of Chinese and English.

item.title: Sora
item.description:
Sora was OpenAI’s attempt to build a general-purpose video model. You described a scene in text, or supplied an image or a clip, and it produced a short video with consistent characters, plausible physics, and controlled camera movement. When it first appeared it was well ahead of most competing video generators, and it later arrived as a standalone social app where people could generate, remix, and share clips.

It could also extend and edit existing footage, blend two clips, and generate several variations of a prompt. The app added features for placing yourself or friends in generated scenes through a consent-based likeness system. That feature drew attention and some controversy over deepfakes, copyright, and who owns the output, and OpenAI had to tighten the rules several times. Generating video also takes a lot of computing power, which made it expensive to run at scale.

item.title: Veo 2
item.description:
Veo 2 generated short high-resolution clips from text or image prompts. It stood out for understanding cinematic language, such as lens choices and camera moves, and for physics that looked plausible, with fewer odd distortions.

It was offered through Google’s creative tools and API before being succeeded by Veo 3, which added native audio and further improvements. Many users moved to the newer model for quality and sound.

Check Google’s documentation for the currently supported models. Alternatives include Veo 3, Runway, Kling, Luma, and Pika. Veo 2 is of interest mainly to people comparing generations of video models.

item.title: Veo 3
item.description:
Veo 3 produces short video clips from text or image prompts with sound included. Earlier video models were silent and required separate audio work; Veo 3 creates speech, effects, and music that match the action, which makes clips feel more complete.

It is available in Google’s Gemini app, in Flow, a filmmaking tool, and through APIs for developers. Filmmakers and marketers use it for concept videos, ads, and social content, and it is known for realistic physics and prompt following.

item.title: Muse Image
item.description:
Muse Image brings Meta’s own image model to its apps. Users describe an image in the Meta AI app, or create pictures in Instagram Stories and WhatsApp, and the model generates it. Meta says the model reasons about a prompt before drawing, rather than mapping text directly to pixels, which helps with complex requests.

Meta plans to extend it to more surfaces, including Facebook, Messenger, and tools for advertisers. Because it is built into apps with billions of users, it makes image creation available to people who would never open a dedicated generator.

item.title: Nano Banana Pro
item.description:
Nano Banana is the name Google gave to its Gemini-based image model, and the Pro version targets higher quality. Users describe an image or edit a photo by instruction, such as changing the background or combining subjects, and the model produces a result that keeps people and objects consistent.

It is known for rendering legible text inside images, producing high-resolution output, and following detailed prompts, which makes it useful for posters, infographics, and product mockups. It is available in the Gemini app, through Google AI Studio and the API, and in other Google products.

item.title: AI for Developers
item.description:
AI for Developers is written for people who build software and want to use AI well. Issues tend to focus on how to do things: setting up an AI coding assistant, writing prompts for common programming tasks, comparing tools, or building small projects with language model APIs. The tone is practical rather than speculative.

A developer-focused newsletter fills a gap between general AI news and academic papers. Readers look for ideas they can apply the same day, such as workflows for code review, testing, or documentation, and for honest comparisons that show what works and what does not. The Substack format also lets readers comment and share tips.

item.title: The Neuron
item.description:
The Neuron is a free email for people who want to follow AI without a technical background. Each issue picks a few stories, explains them in accessible language, and points to tools worth trying. The tone is conversational and avoids excessive jargon.

It includes practical sections, such as prompts and tutorials, and links to its own resources. The newsletter is supported by sponsors, which are labeled.

It is free. As with other daily newsletters, coverage is selective. Alternatives include The Rundown AI, Superhuman AI, TLDR AI, Ben’s Bites, and The Batch. The Neuron suits professionals who want a quick daily AI update.

item.title: The Rundown AI
item.description:
The Rundown AI is one of the most widely read AI newsletters. Each issue covers major stories, new tools, and research in a few minutes of reading, with a consistent format that makes it easy to skim. Sections highlight top stories, quick hits, and tools.

Beyond the newsletter, the brand offers a community, courses, and a product directory. Sponsorship supports the free edition.

The Rundown AI is free. Daily newsletters can repeat the same headlines, so readers often choose one or two. Alternatives include The Neuron, TLDR AI, Superhuman AI, Ben’s Bites, and The Batch. The Rundown AI suits people who want a fast daily briefing.

item.title: Eden AI
item.description:
Eden AI addresses the problem of integrating many AI vendors. Each provider has its own API, formats, and billing. Eden AI offers one API for tasks like text generation, translation, OCR, speech recognition, image analysis, and more, and routes the request to the provider a developer chooses.

That makes comparison simple: the same input can be sent to several providers to see which gives the best result for the price. Fallback options switch to another provider if one fails, and a single bill and dashboard track usage. Workflows allow chaining several AI steps.

item.title: Firecrawl
item.description:
Firecrawl solves a common step in AI projects: getting web content into a form language models can use. A developer gives it a URL, and it fetches the page, handles JavaScript rendering, removes boilerplate, and returns clean Markdown. It can also crawl a whole site, map its links, or extract structured fields from pages using a schema.

Search and agent features expand its use. Developers can search the web and scrape results in one call, or use an endpoint that gathers data across many pages from a plain description. Integrations connect to frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex and to tools via the Model Context Protocol. The core is open source and can be self-hosted.

item.title: Genmo
item.description:
Genmo works on video generation with an open approach. Mochi 1 is a large video model released with open weights, so researchers and developers can study it, run it on their own hardware, and fine-tune it. It was noted for strong motion and for following prompts well among open models at release.

The company also offers a hosted product where users generate clips from text prompts without managing hardware. Creators use it for experimentation, short clips, and concept work. Running the open model locally takes a powerful GPU and some technical skill.

item.title: Haystack
item.description:
Haystack helps developers assemble applications that answer questions over documents. A pipeline strings together components: converting files, splitting text, creating embeddings, retrieving relevant passages, and generating an answer with a language model. Each component is swappable, so teams can change a model or database without rewriting everything.

The framework supports many model providers and vector stores, hybrid search, evaluation tools, and agents that use tools. It also provides a way to serialize pipelines, which supports deployment and testing. deepset offers a commercial platform around it for companies that want managed hosting and collaboration.

item.title: Neon
item.description:
Neon rebuilt Postgres for the cloud by separating storage from compute. That design lets a database scale up under load and scale down to zero when idle, so you pay for use instead of keeping a server running. Developers get standard Postgres, which means existing tools, drivers, and extensions work, including pgvector for storing embeddings in AI applications.

The standout feature is branching. Because storage is copy-on-write, you can create a full copy of a database in seconds, like a Git branch, for testing a migration, running a preview environment for each pull request, or giving each developer an isolated copy. The same ability makes Neon attractive to AI coding agents and platforms that spin up many short-lived databases. Connection pooling, read replicas, and integrations with Vercel and other platforms are available.

item.title: Perplexity Pro
item.description:
Perplexity is an answer engine that searches the web and writes cited responses. The Pro tier raises limits on advanced searches and lets users choose among models, including Perplexity’s own and leading models from other labs, for harder questions.

Pro adds tools for research: upload and analyze documents, longer and more detailed searches, image generation, and access to deeper research modes that produce reports. Spaces let users organize topics and collaborate, and an API credit is sometimes included.

item.title: Vizcom
item.description:
Vizcom speeds up concept design. A designer draws a rough sketch of a shoe, car, or gadget, picks materials or style, and Vizcom generates a realistic render, which can be refined with further drawing and prompts. It can also turn renders into 3D models.

Teams use it to explore many ideas quickly and communicate them to stakeholders. Collaboration tools allow shared workspaces and feedback. Automotive, footwear, and consumer product designers are common users.

item.title: DroneDeploy
item.description:
DroneDeploy is a platform for drone data. Users plan an automated flight from a tablet or phone, the drone captures images, and the software stitches them into orthomosaic maps and 3D models. From these, it can measure distances, areas, and volumes, such as a stockpile or excavation.

Repeat flights show progress. Construction teams compare site conditions to plans, farmers monitor crop health, and mining operations measure material movement. AI detects objects and changes, and the platform has expanded to capture from ground robots and 360 cameras for indoor progress tracking.

item.title: Exscientia
item.description:
Exscientia designed small-molecule drug candidates with AI models and ran automated labs to synthesize and test the top predictions. Results fed back into the models to improve the next round, a closed loop that aimed to shorten discovery time and reduce the number of compounds that must be made.

The company worked on cancer and other diseases, and formed partnerships with large pharmaceutical firms. It was among the first to move AI-designed molecules into clinical trials. After a period of strategic changes, it combined with Recursion, which brought together Recursion’s biology data and Exscientia’s chemistry design and automated synthesis.

item.title: Isomorphic Labs
item.description:
Isomorphic Labs aims to use AI to design medicines. It builds on DeepMind’s work on predicting protein structures and extends the idea to the interactions between proteins and drug molecules, so models can propose compounds that bind to a target. The goal is to reduce the time and cost of finding candidates.

Rather than selling software, the company runs drug discovery programs, both on its own and in collaboration with pharmaceutical companies. It has described building a platform that can be applied across diseases, with early efforts in areas such as oncology and immunology.

item.title: Pearl
item.description:
Pearl focuses on dental radiograph analysis. Dentists upload X-rays, and the Second Opinion tool highlights suspected problems, such as caries, calculus, and periapical lesions, in real time, which helps catch issues and show patients the findings.

The company has expanded into other uses, including claims review for insurers and tools for dental service organizations that want consistent standards across offices. It holds regulatory clearances for several of its functions.

Pearl is sold on subscription to practices and organizations. AI findings need dentist confirmation, and insurers using AI on claims draw scrutiny. Alternatives include Overjet, VideaHealth, Denti.AI, Dentrix Detect, and Align’s tools. Pearl suits dental practices adding AI radiograph review.

item.title: Pix4D
item.description:
Pix4D is photogrammetry software. Photos taken by a drone or a camera are processed into orthomosaics, digital surface models, and 3D meshes with accurate coordinates, so users can measure distances, areas, and volumes from the results.

Products target different jobs. One handles mapping from drones, another focuses on surveying with scanners and phones, and others serve fields like agriculture and inspection. AI helps classify features and clean up point clouds, and cloud processing handles big projects.

item.title: Unit21
item.description:
Unit21 is a risk and compliance platform. It ingests transaction and customer data, flags suspicious activity with rules and machine learning, and routes alerts to analysts through case management. Teams build and adjust rules in a no-code interface.

The platform covers fraud prevention, anti-money laundering monitoring, and onboarding checks, and generates reports such as suspicious activity filings. AI agents help summarize cases and speed investigations.

Unit21 is sold to fintechs, banks, and marketplaces on custom pricing. Alerts need tuning to avoid overload. Alternatives include Sardine, Feedzai, Alloy, ComplyAdvantage, and Actimize. Unit21 suits risk teams at financial companies.

item.title: Appen
item.description:
Appen is one of the long-standing companies behind AI training data. Machine learning models need large amounts of labeled examples, such as transcribed speech, tagged images, ranked answers, and annotated documents, and Appen supplies them through a global crowd of contributors plus managed teams. Its customers have included major technology companies, and its work has fed search, voice assistants, and recommendation systems.

The services now lean toward generative AI. Appen provides data for aligning large language models, such as human preference rankings, expert-written examples, and red-teaming to find unsafe behavior. It also offers multimodal and speech datasets, coding data, and model evaluation services that test how a system performs in many languages and regions. A platform manages the workflows, quality checks, and contributor payments.

item.title: Atomwise
item.description:
Atomwise applies machine learning to the early stage of drug discovery. Its AtomNet technology uses deep learning to predict how well a small molecule would bind to a protein, which lets researchers screen enormous virtual libraries of compounds before running physical experiments. The idea is to cut down the number of molecules a lab has to test, so teams find promising candidates faster and spend less on dead ends.

The company works through partnerships with pharmaceutical firms, biotech startups, and academic labs, covering many disease targets, including some that have been hard to address with conventional methods. Beyond screening, it has developed methods to search ultra-large chemical spaces and tools for designing and optimizing compounds. It also runs internal programs, so it is both a technology provider and a drug developer.

item.title: Augury
item.description:
Augury helps factories and facilities avoid unexpected equipment failures. Small wireless sensors attach to machines such as motors, pumps, fans, and compressors and measure vibration, temperature, and other signals. The data goes to the cloud, where machine learning models trained on large numbers of machines identify patterns that signal a developing problem, such as bearing wear or misalignment, often weeks before a breakdown.

The platform sends alerts with a diagnosis and recommended action, so maintenance teams can plan repairs during scheduled downtime instead of reacting to a failure. Dashboards show the health of assets across plants, and the service has expanded to include process monitoring and insights into production performance. Industries include food and beverage, chemicals, pulp and paper, and building management.

item.title: Autodesk Construction Cloud
item.description:
Autodesk Construction Cloud brings together the tools that general contractors, owners, and subcontractors use to run building projects. A shared data environment keeps drawings, models, and documents in one place with version control, so everyone works from the current set. Teams use it for design review, model coordination across disciplines, quantity takeoff, cost estimating, issue tracking, and quality and safety checks in the field.

Autodesk has been folding the product line into Forma, its industry cloud, and the construction products now carry the Forma name, such as Forma Build, Forma Data Management, Forma Takeoff, and Forma Estimate. They connect to Autodesk’s design tools like Revit, which keeps information flowing from the design model to the construction site. AI features help automate routine work and surface insights, for example by flagging risks, extracting information from documents, or speeding up takeoff.

item.title: AWS Rekognition
item.description: Rekognition lets developers add image and video analysis to an application without training a model from scratch. You send an image or a video and get back detected objects and scenes, text found in the picture, faces with attributes such as glasses or smiling, and flags for unsafe or inappropriate content. It works on photos, stored video files, and live video streams, and it integrates with S3, Lambda, and other AWS services.

item.title: Azure Content Moderator
item.description:
Content Moderator was Microsoft’s tool for checking user-generated content. It scanned text for profanity and personal data, analyzed images for adult or racy content, and screened video, returning scores and flags that platforms could use to filter or send items for human review. Online communities, marketplaces, and apps with user uploads used it as an automated first line of defense.

Microsoft has deprecated the service and no longer allows new projects, directing customers to Azure AI Content Safety. The newer service uses more advanced models, handles multiple severity levels across categories such as hate, sexual content, violence, and self-harm, supports many more languages, and adds features aimed at generative AI, including prompt shields and groundedness detection. Existing Content Moderator projects continue to work until the retirement date.

item.title: Bambu Studio
item.description:
Bambu Studio turns 3D model files into instructions a printer can follow. You load a model, arrange it on the virtual build plate, set options such as layer height, supports, and infill, and the slicer generates the toolpath, previewing how the print will be built. It supports multicolor and multimaterial printing through Bambu’s automatic material system, with tools to assign colors and manage waste.

It is based on open-source slicer code and is itself open source. Features include automatic calibration, print profiles tuned for Bambu printers and common filaments, remote monitoring and control over the cloud, and integration with MakerWorld, Bambu’s online library of models, where users share designs and print profiles. It runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux and also supports some other printers.

item.title: Be My Eyes
item.description: Be My Eyes connects people who cannot see well with help. In the app, a blind or low-vision user can start a video call, and a sighted volunteer sees through the camera and helps with a task such as reading an expiry date, matching colors, finding a dropped item, or navigating an unfamiliar place. Millions of volunteers around the world have signed up, which means that help is usually available quickly, at any hour.

item.title: BetterHelp
item.description:
BetterHelp is one of the largest online therapy platforms. You fill out a questionnaire about your needs and preferences, and the service suggests a licensed counselor. You can message your therapist, join live sessions by video, phone, or chat, and schedule at times that suit you, which removes commuting and makes weekly care easier for many people. Therapists are independent licensed professionals such as psychologists, social workers, and counselors.

The pricing model is a recurring subscription based on location and therapist, rather than per-visit billing, and it generally does not accept insurance, which some people find convenient and others find expensive. It is owned by Teladoc Health. Some reviewers praise the convenience and access, while others report difficulty finding a good match or a pushy sales process. Therapy that happens in messages works differently from a weekly hour in an office, and some people prefer live sessions.

item.title: Bonterra
item.description:
Bonterra was created by combining several nonprofit software companies, including EveryAction, Social Solutions, Network for Good, and CyberGrants. That heritage explains the breadth: the company sells tools for fundraising and donor management, case management for human services programs, volunteer and employee giving programs, grants administration, and online giving pages. Nonprofits can use pieces of it or adopt a larger suite.

The pitch is to connect the work of raising money with the work of delivering programs. A charity can track a donor’s giving next to the services it funds, and a case manager can record outcomes that feed into reports for funders. AI features appear in tasks like drafting fundraising messages, segmenting supporters, and summarizing case notes, with attention to privacy because the data can be sensitive.

item.title: Clarifai
item.description: Clarifai started as an image recognition API and has grown into a broader AI platform. Teams use it to find and call models for vision, language, and audio tasks, to train their own models on labeled data, and to run them in production. It includes tools for organizing and labeling data, searching images and video, and building workflows that chain several models together. Industries such as retail, media, and public sector have used it to classify content and find objects in large collections.

item.title: Covariant
item.description: Covariant started in robotics research with a goal of building a general model that could control robots in the physical world. Its first big application was robotic picking, in which a robot arm takes products from bins and places them into orders. That task is hard because warehouses contain thousands of different items with varied shapes, materials, and packaging. Covariant Brain, its AI system, was trained on data from many deployments to deal with that variety, instead of being programmed for each product.

item.title: Fauna
item.description:
Fauna set out to give developers a database that scaled globally without managing servers. It combined a flexible document model with relational features, offered strong consistency across regions, and was accessed through an API with its own query language, FQL, and earlier through GraphQL. Developers built web and mobile apps on it without running infrastructure.

The company announced that it would wind down its hosted service, and the service closed, with accounts deleted afterward. It also said it would release parts of its technology as open source, so some of the ideas may live on in community projects.

item.title: FlowGPT
item.description:
FlowGPT started as a place to share ChatGPT prompts. People post prompts for writing, coding, productivity, roleplay, and other uses, and others can browse by category, upvote the best, and copy them. Over time it added the ability to run prompts directly on the site and to build small chatbot-style apps, so a prompt can become a reusable tool.

The community aspect drives it. Creators gain followers and recognition for popular prompts, and the site hosts character chats and templates for tasks such as resume writing or SEO. It offers a way to learn prompting techniques by examining what others have written. Many of the contributions are playful or experimental, with quality that varies.

item.title: Hive Moderation
item.description:
Hive offers content moderation as an API. A platform sends user uploads, such as photos, videos, livestreams, comments, or audio, and Hive returns classifications with confidence scores across categories like nudity, violence, hate symbols, drugs, and self-harm. Companies use these results to automatically remove content, send borderline cases to human reviewers, or restrict access, which would be impossible to do manually at scale.

The company’s models have broadened beyond traditional moderation. Hive offers AI-generated content detection to identify synthetic images, video, and audio, deepfake detection used by government and media customers, and tools for brand safety and contextual advertising. It trains on large human-labeled datasets, and customers can customize settings for their own policies.

item.title: Iris Dating
item.description:
Iris Dating tries to reduce the mismatch of attraction. Users swipe on photos, and the system learns their visual preferences, then predicts which other users they would find attractive and shows only those who are likely to find them attractive as well. The aim is fewer, better matches.

The approach uses facial recognition and machine learning on profile photos, which raises privacy questions about how biometric data is processed and stored. Users should read the policy before uploading photos. Dating apps also carry safety concerns, so meet in public places and verify identities.

item.title: Labelbox
item.description:
Labelbox helps AI teams turn raw data into labeled datasets. Its tools let annotators draw boxes and masks on images and video, tag text, transcribe audio, and rate model responses. Project management features assign work, review quality, and measure agreement between labelers, so teams can catch mistakes early. The platform supports both in-house labelers and external workforces.

The company has focused on generative AI. Tools support reinforcement learning from human feedback and model evaluation, where experts compare and rank responses, and a labeling service provides specialist annotators for domains such as coding, math, and medicine. Model-assisted labeling uses a model to pre-label data so humans only correct it, and data curation tools help find the most valuable examples. Integrations connect with cloud storage and ML pipelines.

item.title: Landing AI
item.description:
Landing AI is built around data-centric AI, the idea that improving the quality of training data often matters more than tweaking models. Its LandingLens platform lets manufacturing, agriculture, and healthcare teams train computer vision models for tasks like detecting defects, counting objects, and classifying images, with a no-code interface that emphasizes labeling quality and error analysis. Domain experts can build models without being machine learning engineers.

The company has expanded into document intelligence. Its agentic document extraction uses vision and language models to read complex documents such as financial statements, forms, and reports, and to turn them into structured data with visual grounding that shows where each value came from. Developers use APIs to add this to workflows.

item.title: Lemonade
item.description:
Lemonade is an insurance company built around software. Customers get a quote and buy a policy in minutes through an app, chatting with an AI assistant called Maya instead of filling out long forms. The company covers renters, homeowners, car, pet, and term life insurance in various markets. Its pitch to younger customers has been a modern experience, low entry prices, and transparent terms.

AI shows up in operations. A claims bot named Jim can approve and pay simple claims quickly, sometimes within seconds, while complex cases go to human adjusters.
