Machine learning helps assess risk, detect fraud, and personalize pricing. The company is structured so that it takes a flat fee and uses the rest to pay claims, with unused money going to charities chosen by customers under its Giveback program.

item.title: MonkeyLearn
item.description:
MonkeyLearn let people analyze text without machine learning expertise. Teams could connect support tickets, survey responses, reviews, and social posts, pick a ready-made model for sentiment or topics, or train a custom classifier by tagging examples. Results appeared in dashboards and could be sent to spreadsheets, helpdesks, and BI tools, which made it popular with customer experience, product, and marketing teams.

Its approach was to make natural language processing approachable. A visual interface handled model creation and testing, and the API let developers add analysis to their own apps. Typical uses included tagging support requests by issue, tracking sentiment in reviews, and pulling themes from open-ended survey answers.

item.title: OneTrust
item.description:
OneTrust helps large organizations manage the rules about data. Its best-known product handles consent: the cookie banners and preference centers that appear on websites and apps and record what visitors agree to. Privacy teams use other modules to respond to data subject requests such as access and deletion, map where personal data is stored, run privacy impact assessments, and show regulators that they follow laws like GDPR and CCPA.

The platform has expanded into broader governance, risk, and compliance. Tools cover third-party and vendor risk, security and IT risk, ethics and policy management, and environmental and social reporting. A growing area is AI governance: inventorying the AI systems an organization uses, assessing their risks, and tracking compliance with emerging rules such as the EU AI Act. AI features in the platform help classify data and automate assessments.

item.title: Petcube
item.description:
Petcube sells connected cameras for people who want to check on pets while away. A camera with a wide-angle view streams video to a phone app, and two-way audio lets owners talk to the pet. Models differ in features: some include a built-in laser toy for play, some toss treats on command, and some are designed for indoor or outdoor use. Setup is through Wi-Fi and a smartphone.

Software adds intelligence. AI can detect when a pet is barking, moving, or when a person is in view, and send alerts, and a subscription provides cloud recording, event history, and access to veterinarians by video chat. Pet owners use it to keep an eye on anxious dogs, monitor cats, and share live views with family members.

item.title: PromptHero
item.description:
PromptHero started as a search engine for AI image prompts. You can browse a huge gallery of generated images, each shown with the prompt and settings that created it, and search for styles or subjects. That makes it a learning tool: you can see how others phrase things to get a certain look, and adapt their prompts to your own ideas.

The site has added features around the community. Users upload their creations, follow artists, and join challenges, and a generator lets you create images directly on the site using several models. Courses and guides teach prompt writing and workflow tips for different tools, and a paid tier offers more generations and features.

item.title: Recursion Pharmaceuticals
item.description: Recursion approaches drug discovery as a data problem. Its labs run enormous numbers of experiments in which cells are treated with genetic changes or compounds and photographed under microscopes. Machine learning analyzes the images to find how diseases change cell appearance and which compounds reverse those changes, building a large map of biology that the company calls the Recursion OS. The idea is to find promising targets and molecules faster than with traditional trial-and-error screening.

item.title: Root Insurance
item.description:
Root built its pitch on the idea that safe drivers should pay less. New customers take a test drive period with the app, which uses the phone’s sensors to measure things such as braking, speed, turning, and time of day driving. Combined with other information, those readings help set the price, so a careful driver can get a lower rate than under traditional pricing based mainly on demographics.

The process is online. People get a quote, buy a policy, and manage their coverage in the app, including proof of insurance and claims. Root also sells through partners, embedding insurance into other companies’ purchasing flows, and has added products such as renters insurance. Machine learning supports pricing, fraud detection, and claims handling.

item.title: Sight Machine
item.description:
Sight Machine tackles the data mess inside factories. Machines, sensors, and systems produce data in many formats, and plants often cannot easily combine it. Sight Machine’s platform pulls in data from equipment, quality systems, and enterprise software, standardizes it into a common model of the production process, and creates a digital twin that shows how products move through the plant.

With that foundation, teams can analyze performance. Dashboards track throughput, yield, scrap, and downtime across lines and sites, machine learning finds the factors that drive defects or slowdowns, and alerts flag issues in near real time. An AI assistant lets operators and engineers ask questions about production data in plain language, and the platform supports sustainability tracking such as energy use.

item.title: Transcend
item.description:
Transcend takes a developer-oriented approach to privacy compliance. It connects to a company’s databases, SaaS tools, and warehouses to discover where personal data is stored, then automates responses to requests from individuals to access or delete their data. Instead of manually searching dozens of systems, the platform executes the request across them and keeps a record.

Other products cover related needs. Consent management controls cookies and tracking according to each visitor’s choices and location, a gateway can enforce those choices in what data flows to third parties, and data mapping documents processing activities. Newer tools address AI governance, helping teams track what data feeds models and meet emerging regulations.

item.title: Ultimaker Cura
item.description:
Cura converts 3D models into printer instructions. Users load a model, position it, choose a material and quality profile, and the software slices it into layers, with a preview that shows how the print will be built. Settings control supports, infill, speed, temperature, and more, and a simple mode hides complexity for beginners while a custom mode exposes hundreds of options.

It has a very large user base because it works with many printers, not only those made by UltiMaker. Community-maintained profiles cover popular brands, and a plugin marketplace adds features such as post-processing scripts and cloud integrations. Cura is developed in the open and has had long-running support from the maker community.

item.title: AI For Developer
item.description:
AI For Developer is a niche directory focused on the developer audience. Instead of listing every AI product, it gathers tools that matter to people who write software: coding assistants, AI-powered editors, model APIs, testing and documentation tools, and infrastructure for building AI features. Listings give a short description, links, and categories, which makes it easy to browse by use case.

Directories like this serve as a starting point for discovery. They help developers learn what exists, compare similar tools, and keep up with the rapid pace of new launches. A curated approach aims to reduce the noise of general AI directories that include thousands of products across every field, by focusing on relevance to engineering.

item.title: AIDir.wiki
item.description:
AIDir.wiki collects information about AI products in a wiki format. Each entry describes a tool or model, notes what it is for, lists key features and pricing information, and links to the official site. Because it is community-maintained, contributors can add new tools and update existing entries as products change, which is meant to keep information fresher than a static list.

The wiki structure encourages cross-linking, so related tools, alternatives, and categories connect. Visitors can browse by category or search for a specific product, and use it as a reference when comparing options. It joins a broad field of AI directories, from curated lists to large databases, and positions itself as an open, collaborative resource.

item.title: AIVE
item.description:
AIVE was described as a video enhancement service that used deep-learning super-resolution to sharpen detail, reduce noise, and raise the resolution of existing footage. That kind of tool takes low-resolution or damaged video, such as old family tapes, archival film, or compressed web clips, and reconstructs a clearer version. The idea is sound, and a number of products do it well.

The domain listed for AIVE no longer hosts a video enhancement tool. It now shows an unrelated media site, and searches turn up no active product of this name with the features described. A separate company called Aive makes a platform for automating video post-production for brands, which is a different kind of product. Because the original service cannot be confirmed, this entry should not be used as a recommendation.

item.title: Altern
item.description:
Altern is a browsable directory of AI products. Visitors can search by task or browse categories, such as writing, design, coding, and video, and see short descriptions, pricing, links, and user ratings. Rankings and filters aim to surface popular and well-regarded tools so people do not have to sift through thousands of options alone.

Tool makers can submit their products to be listed, and users can leave ratings and reviews. The directory also offers comparisons and alternatives for specific products, which is useful when you already know one tool and want to see similar ones. Like other discovery sites, it covers a wide range from established products to new launches.

item.title: Andi
item.description:
Andi is a search engine for people who find link lists cluttered. You ask a question, and it returns a short answer with cited sources, plus links you can open. The idea is to combine the answering ability of a language model with the freshness of the web.

Privacy and design are part of the pitch. Andi has said it does not rely on advertising or sell user data, and the interface is clean, with options to refine a query and explore related questions. It is one of several startups, along with Perplexity, You.com, and Phind, that took on the conventional search model.

item.title: AnythingLLM
item.description:
AnythingLLM gives you a private place to talk to your files. You add documents, web pages, or other content to a workspace, and the app indexes them in a vector database. When you ask a question, it retrieves relevant passages and sends them to a language model, which answers with references.

Flexibility is the main draw. You can choose a local model through Ollama or LM Studio, or a cloud model from providers such as OpenAI and Anthropic, and swap them without rebuilding your workspace. It has agents that can browse the web or run tools, supports multiple users and permissions in the server version, and offers an API and embeddable chat widget.

item.title: Artbreeder
item.description: Artbreeder began with an unusual idea: instead of typing a prompt, you start with existing images and breed them together, like mixing genes. Each image has sliders for traits, such as age, expression, or lighting for a portrait, so you can nudge it in a direction and save the results. Children of images can be crossed again, which lets a visual idea evolve step by step. The community shares images that others can remix.

item.title: Attention Insight
item.description: Attention Insight offers an inexpensive shortcut to a classic design question: will anyone notice this? Upload a screenshot, ad, packaging mockup, or video, and its AI produces a heatmap of the areas likely to draw the eye in the first few seconds. The model is trained on eye-tracking data, so the predictions approximate what real viewers would do. It returns results in seconds, which makes it practical to compare several versions of a design.

item.title: Blue Yonder
item.description: Blue Yonder helps companies plan and run their supply chains. Demand forecasting predicts what customers will buy, inventory planning decides how much stock to hold and where, and transportation and warehouse systems manage how goods move. Retailers, manufacturers, and logistics providers use it to balance supply and demand, reduce stockouts and excess inventory, and respond to disruptions. The company grew from JDA Software and acquired an AI startup that gave it its name.

item.title: Brave Leo
item.description: Leo sits in the browser’s sidebar and works with whatever page you are viewing. You can ask it to summarize an article or a long video transcript, explain a technical passage, extract key points from a PDF, or answer questions about the content, without copying text into a separate chatbot. It can also help write or rewrite text, translate, brainstorm, and answer general questions, with the option of using the web for current information.

item.title: Carnegie Learning
item.description: Carnegie Learning grew out of research at Carnegie Mellon University on how people learn math. Its flagship product, MATHia, is an intelligent tutoring system that watches how a student solves each step of a problem, estimates which skills the student has mastered, and adjusts the next problem and hints accordingly. The aim is to give every student something like a personal tutor, with feedback at the moment a mistake occurs.

item.title: Codeium
item.description: Codeium started as a free alternative to GitHub Copilot, offering code completion and chat in more than 40 editors, among them VS Code, JetBrains IDEs, Vim, and Neovim. Its free individual tier and wide editor support earned it a large user base among developers who did not want to pay for a coding assistant or switch editors. It added features such as natural-language code search, in-editor chat, and support for dozens of programming languages.

item.title: Composio
item.description:
Composio is an integration layer for AI agents. Agents need to take actions in other software, which means handling authentication and API details for each service. Composio supplies a catalog of connectors that handle sign-in flows and expose actions in a form models can call, so a developer can give an agent access to many apps with a few lines of code.

It works with agent frameworks and model providers, supports the Model Context Protocol, and manages user authorization so that agents act on behalf of each end user. Tools for monitoring let developers see what actions agents took, and permissions limit what an agent can do.

item.title: Coze
item.description:
Coze lets non-programmers build conversational agents. In its editor, you describe the bot’s role and behavior, choose a language model, and attach tools: plugins for web search, image generation, and other services, plus knowledge bases that hold your documents. Visual workflows chain steps together for more complex tasks, and memory features let a bot recall details about users. A store lets creators share and discover bots built by others.

Publishing is flexible. A finished agent can be deployed to messaging apps and chat platforms, embedded on a website, or exposed through an API, which makes it practical for customer support, community bots, personal assistants, and internal tools. ByteDance has also released parts of the platform as open source for those who want to run it themselves, and offers separate editions for different regions.

item.title: dbt Cloud
item.description:
dbt, short for data build tool, became the standard way to transform raw data inside a warehouse such as Snowflake, BigQuery, or Databricks. Analysts write SQL select statements, define dependencies among them, and dbt builds tables and views in the right order, with version control, testing, and documentation. This brings software engineering practices like code review and continuous integration to analytics work.

dbt Cloud is the hosted product from dbt Labs. It provides a browser-based IDE, job scheduling, CI that tests changes before they reach production, a data catalog with lineage, and a semantic layer that defines metrics once for use across BI tools. AI features help generate models, tests, and documentation, and answer questions about the project, which speeds up repetitive tasks.

item.title: Feedzai
item.description:
Feedzai provides real-time fraud detection for banks, card issuers, and payment companies. Its models look at each transaction along with customer and device behavior and decide in milliseconds whether to approve, block, or send it for review. Flagging account takeover, card fraud, and scams quickly limits losses.

The platform also covers anti-money laundering and customer risk, combining signals from different parts of a bank in a single view. Case management tools help investigators work alerts, and explainability features show why a decision was made, which matters to regulators. Newer work addresses authorized scams where customers are tricked into sending money.

item.title: Fly.io
item.description:
Fly.io lets developers deploy applications near their users. You package an app, often as a Docker container, and Fly runs it in lightweight virtual machines called Machines in many cities, which reduces latency compared with a single centralized region. A command-line tool handles deployment, scaling, and configuration, so a small team can get a global application running without managing servers.

The platform has features useful for modern applications. Machines can start quickly and stop when idle, which suits workloads that spike, private networking links services securely, and volumes provide persistent storage. Managed Postgres and other data services are available, and GPU instances support AI workloads. It’s popular with developers using frameworks such as Rails, Phoenix, Django, and Laravel.

item.title: Forethought AI
item.description: Forethought applies AI to the work that fills support queues. It reads incoming tickets and classifies them by topic and urgency, routes them to the right team, and drafts answers for human agents using the company’s knowledge base and past tickets. For common questions, its AI agents answer directly in chat and email and take simple actions such as checking an order status, handing off to a person when they cannot resolve the issue.

item.title: Gemini Advanced
item.description:
Gemini Advanced was Google’s answer to ChatGPT Plus. When Google rebranded Bard as Gemini, it introduced Advanced as a subscription, sold through Google One, that gave access to its strongest model, longer conversations, and features like file uploads and integration with Gmail and Docs. It also bundled extra Google One storage, which made it attractive to people already paying for cloud storage.

Google later reorganized the plans. Gemini Advanced’s features moved into Google AI Pro, and a higher tier called Google AI Ultra provides the most advanced models, agent features, and generous limits for heavy users. The plans include perks such as video generation, deeper research tools, and integrations with Workspace apps, and the exact lineup changes with each product update.

item.title: Gen-2
item.description:
Runway builds generative video tools for filmmakers, designers, and creators. Gen-3 Alpha was a major step in its line, generating short clips from a text prompt or an image with better detail, motion, and consistency than earlier versions. It supported controls for camera movement and style.

Runway’s platform around its models includes editing tools, motion brush features, and ways to extend or modify clips. Its research focuses on world models and video generation for creative work, and the company works with studios and artists. The newer models in the line have largely taken the place of Gen-3.

item.title: Gong
item.description:
Gong captures sales conversations and turns them into insight. It records calls and meetings, transcribes them, and pulls in emails and CRM data, then analyzes what is happening across the pipeline: which topics come up in deals that close, how often competitors are mentioned, how much reps talk compared with customers, and where deals are stalling. Managers can search a library of calls instead of relying on reps’ summaries.

The AI features save time at several levels. Calls are summarized with key points and next steps, which are written back to the CRM. Deal boards highlight risks, such as no recent contact with a decision-maker, and forecasting tools estimate which deals will close. Coaching tools find moments to review and compare behavior across reps, and newer AI agents help with tasks such as preparing for meetings, researching accounts, and drafting follow-ups.

item.title: GPTZero
item.description: GPTZero was created by a Princeton student soon after ChatGPT appeared and became one of the most used AI detectors. You paste text or upload a document, and it returns the probability that the writing is human or AI, with sentences highlighted by likelihood. It looks at features such as perplexity and burstiness, which describe how predictable and varied the writing is, and uses trained models for classification. Teachers, editors, and publishers use it to flag content for a closer look.

item.title: Harvey
item.description:
Harvey was built for lawyers and has become one of the best-known legal AI companies. Attorneys use its assistant to ask legal questions, draft and revise contracts and memos, summarize documents, and analyze large sets of files, such as the documents in a due diligence review. It runs on leading language models adapted for legal work and is designed to provide citations so lawyers can verify the answers.

Beyond a chat assistant, Harvey offers structured features. Vault stores and analyzes large document collections, workflows automate multi-step tasks such as contract review against a playbook, and integrations connect with tools law firms already use, including document management and legal research providers. Firms can customize the system with their own templates and precedents, and security controls support the confidentiality requirements of legal practice.

item.title: Hugging Face
item.description: Hugging Face is often described as the GitHub of machine learning. Researchers and companies upload models and datasets to its Hub, where anyone can browse them, read the documentation, and download them. If an open model is released, whether a language model, an image generator, or a speech system, it almost always appears there first. Each model page has a card describing what it does, how it was trained, and how to use it, along with community discussions.

item.title: iNaturalist
item.description:
iNaturalist is a citizen science project and app. Users upload photos or sounds of organisms they find, a computer vision model suggests what species it is, and other observers weigh in. When enough people agree, the observation reaches research grade, and the data is shared with scientific databases.

The result is one of the largest collections of biodiversity observations. Researchers use it to track species ranges, detect invasive species, and study changes over time. Projects and bioblitz events organize community efforts, and schools use it for nature education.

item.title: Kagi
item.description:
Kagi takes a different business model from other search engines: users pay a subscription, and in return there are no ads, no tracking-based profiles, and no incentive to favor advertisers. Results are meant to be clean and relevant, and the company says it does not sell data. The service uses several sources, including its own index of smaller sites, and puts effort into reducing low-quality content and SEO spam.

Control is a defining feature. Users can raise, lower, or block domains, so a site that is always useless for you disappears, and lenses restrict a search to a set of sources, such as forums or academic sites. AI tools include summaries of pages and videos, answers with citations, and an assistant that gives access to multiple language models. Kagi has also launched Orion, a privacy-focused browser, and other products around the search experience.

item.title: Kasisto
item.description:
Kasisto builds AI assistants for banks. Its KAI technology understands banking questions and can carry out actions, such as showing recent transactions, transferring funds, or explaining a fee, in a chat within a bank’s mobile app or website. The language models are tuned to the vocabulary and rules of finance.

A newer product, KAI Answers, uses generative AI to answer questions from a bank’s own policies and documents, with citations so staff and customers can see the source. Banks use it to cut call volumes and improve self-service, and the company has worked with institutions around the world.

item.title: Kensho
item.description:
Kensho began as a startup applying machine learning to financial markets and was acquired by S&P Global, where it operates as the company’s AI innovation hub. Its products address practical data problems in finance. Kensho Link matches records between data sets, such as linking company names across different sources, Kensho Classify tags documents by category, and Kensho Extract pulls data out of PDFs and filings.

More recent work connects financial data to generative AI. Kensho develops tools that allow AI assistants and agents to access S&P Global’s data reliably, with grounding that provides sources for answers, plus language models and benchmarks for finance. Its technology supports S&P products and is available to clients who want to build their own applications.

item.title: Kimi
item.description:
Kimi first gained attention for handling very long documents. Users can upload large PDFs, books, or collections of files and ask questions, and the assistant keeps track of the whole text, which suited tasks like summarizing reports and analyzing contracts. It also searches the web, writes and reasons about code, and has agent features that carry out multi-step tasks.

Moonshot AI releases powerful models, including open-weight versions of its Kimi K2 family, which are among the larger open models and strong at coding and agentic tasks. Developers use them through Moonshot’s API or run them through third-party providers, and they are often used inside coding tools. The company competes with other Chinese labs such as DeepSeek, Alibaba, and Zhipu.

item.title: LangChain
item.description: LangChain gave developers a common toolkit when language models first became available through APIs. It supplies building blocks for the typical parts of an AI application: calling a model, formatting prompts, parsing outputs, connecting to tools and data sources, and keeping memory of a conversation. Because it supports many model providers and vector stores behind consistent interfaces, you can swap one for another with little code change. Python and JavaScript versions are available.

item.title: Le Chat
item.description:
Le Chat is Mistral’s answer to ChatGPT and Claude. The French company designed the app for general use: answering questions, writing and editing, summarizing documents, analyzing images, generating images, and running code. Fast response modes make it quick for everyday queries, and a canvas supports working on documents and code beside the chat.

Further features address more advanced needs. Deep research compiles longer reports from web sources, connectors link to services like Gmail, Google Drive, and Notion, and custom agents let users set up specialized assistants. Memory can retain preferences between chats, and mobile apps bring it to phones. The assistant uses Mistral’s own models, some of which are open-weight, and emphasizes European hosting and privacy options.

item.title: Llamasoft
item.description:
Llamasoft helped companies answer strategic supply chain questions. Where should factories and warehouses be placed? How would costs change if a port closes or demand shifts? Its software builds a digital model of a supply network, then uses optimization and simulation to test alternatives and recommend the best configuration, balancing cost, service levels, and risk. Large manufacturers, retailers, and consumer goods companies used it for network design and planning.

Coupa acquired Llamasoft and folded it into its business spend management platform, so customers can connect supply chain decisions with procurement and spend data. The technology continues under Coupa branding, with capabilities such as network optimization, inventory and sourcing analysis, and demand sensing, supported by machine learning and a digital twin of the supply chain.

item.title: Mage.space
item.description:
Mage.space gives people a simple front end for open-source image models. You choose from a catalog of checkpoints, write a prompt, adjust settings like style, size, and number of images, and generate. It supports image-to-image transformations, inpainting, and control features that guide composition, and results can be upscaled. Because it hosts the models, users do not need a powerful computer or a local installation.

The platform appeals to people who want flexibility in styles, from realistic photos to anime and fantasy art, and who want to experiment with community-trained models. It has a gallery of public creations, and a text-to-video tool has been added to some plans. Content rules are looser than on some mainstream services, though it still prohibits illegal material.

item.title: Masterpiece Studio
item.description:
Masterpiece Studio began with virtual reality tools for sculpting, painting, and animating in 3D, making 3D creation more intuitive for artists. It later moved toward generative AI, with Masterpiece X, which generates 3D models from text or images. Users describe an object, and the system produces a mesh with textures that can be refined or used as a starting point for game assets, virtual worlds, and prototypes.

The aim is to make output useful in production. Generated models can be downloaded in common formats and used in game engines such as Unity and Unreal, or opened in Blender and other tools for editing. Additional features help with rigging and animation, so characters can be posed and moved without a complex setup. A no-code approach targets creators who do not have a modeling background, including developers and designers who need many assets.

item.title: Meshcapade
item.description:
Meshcapade grew out of research at the Max Planck Institute on how to represent human bodies in 3D. Its core is SMPL, a parametric model that describes body shape and pose with a small set of numbers, which makes it efficient to generate and animate realistic humans. SMPL has become widely used in computer vision and graphics research, and Meshcapade commercializes the technology.

Its products turn images and video into 3D human data. Motion capture from ordinary video can extract body movement without suits or special cameras, and the output can be used in animation, games, virtual production, and sports analysis. Tools generate avatars with accurate body shapes for virtual try-on in fashion, health and fitness applications, and digital humans. An API lets developers integrate these capabilities, and plugins connect with popular 3D software.

item.title: Meta AI
item.description: Meta AI is the assistant that Meta put where its users already are. In WhatsApp, Instagram, Messenger, and Facebook, you can mention it in a chat or open it from the search bar to ask a question, get recommendations, or generate an image. There is also a standalone app and website with fuller features, including natural voice conversations, image creation and editing, and a feed where people share what they have made.

item.title: Modal
item.description:
Modal removes much of the setup around running compute. A developer writes Python, adds decorators that say what hardware and packages are needed, and Modal builds the container, starts it on demand, scales to many machines, and shuts it down when finished. Startup is fast, which makes it practical for bursty workloads.

Typical uses include model inference, fine-tuning, batch jobs, data processing, and running sandboxes for agents. Features such as web endpoints, scheduled jobs, volumes for storage, and notebooks cover a range of needs. Pricing is based on seconds of compute.

item.title: Mosaic
item.description:
Mosaic is aimed at finance teams that want a modern view of the business. It pulls data from accounting systems, sales tools, and HR platforms into a single model, so metrics like revenue, headcount, and cash are current and consistent. Teams build reports and board decks from live data.

Forecasting and scenario tools let teams test assumptions, such as hiring plans or pricing changes, and see the impact. AI allows users to ask questions in plain language and get analysis, and automates routine commentary and variance explanations.

item.title: Obsidian
item.description: Obsidian treats notes as local files. Everything you write is a Markdown document in a folder on your computer, so you own the data and can open it with any other editor. You connect notes with links, and the app shows backlinks and a graph view of how ideas relate. People use it for personal knowledge management, research, writing, journaling, and project notes, and many build large networks of thousands of linked notes over years.

item.title: Opendoor
item.description:
Opendoor popularized the iBuyer model. A homeowner enters an address and details, receives an offer within days based on the company’s pricing model and an inspection, and can close on a timeline they choose. The company then repairs and resells the home. The process appeals to sellers who value speed and certainty over getting the highest price.

Technology is central to the business. Machine learning models estimate what a home is worth and how long it will take to sell, using data on the property and the local market, and these estimates determine offers and risk. Opendoor also offers listing options for sellers who prefer to sell traditionally, along with buyer services such as touring homes with self-guided access in some markets.

item.title: OpenRouter
item.description:
OpenRouter solves the problem of juggling many AI provider accounts. A developer gets one API key and one endpoint, and can call any supported model by changing its name, using the same request format as OpenAI’s API. Billing is unified, with credits that work across providers, which makes it easy to try new models as soon as they appear, including open-source ones hosted by different companies.

Beyond routing, it adds useful features. Automatic fallbacks switch to another provider if one is down, routing options choose the cheapest or fastest provider for a model, and analytics show usage and cost. Public rankings show which models people use most, giving a view of real-world adoption. Users can bring their own provider keys and set data privacy preferences that control which providers may see their prompts.

item.title: Originality.ai
item.description:
Originality.ai was built for people who commission or publish written content and want to know whether it was written by AI. You paste text or scan a URL, and it returns a score estimating the likelihood the text was generated by models such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, alongside a plagiarism check against web sources. Content teams, SEO agencies, and website buyers use it to check contractors’ work.

Additional tools include a fact-checking aid, a readability analysis, and a feature that shows the writing history of a Google Doc to demonstrate how it was composed. A Chrome extension and API support integration with publishing workflows, and team accounts allow reviewing many pieces. The company publishes accuracy studies, although its results are disputed by others.

item.title: Perplexity AI
item.description:
Perplexity positions itself as an alternative to the list of links. You ask a question in natural language, it searches the web in real time, reads the pages, and writes a concise answer with citations to each source. That format is helpful for questions where you want a quick overview with a way to check the evidence, such as product comparisons, news, how-to questions, and research basics.

The experience supports continued exploration. Follow-up questions build on earlier context, and focus options narrow the search to categories such as academic sources or discussion forums. Pro Search runs more steps for complex questions, and Deep Research generates longer reports. The Comet browser brings the assistant into everyday browsing, and Spaces organize related research. Users can choose among several models in paid plans.

item.title: Perplexity Labs
item.description: Labs goes beyond answering a question. You describe a project, such as a market analysis, a financial model, or a small dashboard, and Labs works for several minutes, combining web research, code execution, and chart creation. It then returns finished assets: a written report, a spreadsheet, charts, or a simple web app that you can download or share. The tool uses a team of specialized steps behind the scenes, so the output is more like a deliverable than a chat reply.

item.title: Pika Labs
item.description: Pika grew popular by making AI video fun and easy for people with no editing experience. You type a prompt or upload an image, and it generates a short clip in a few moments. Its signature features are effects that change objects in playful ways, such as melting, squishing, inflating, or turning something into cake, which spread quickly across social media. The interface is simple and mobile-friendly, which suited creators who make clips for TikTok and Instagram.

item.title: Pika Labs
item.description:
Pika makes short video easy. A user types a prompt, uploads an image, or provides a clip, and Pika generates or modifies footage. It is known for playful effects, like making objects melt or inflate, as well as realistic motion and camera control.

Creators use it for social posts, ads, and concept work. Features include editing parts of a video, extending clips, adding sound, and lip sync. The platform has expanded to support multiple underlying models and mobile apps.

item.title: Pinecone
item.description:
Pinecone provides the storage and search layer for applications that work with embeddings, which are numerical representations of text, images, or other data. A developer converts documents into vectors, stores them in Pinecone, and later retrieves the ones closest in meaning to a query. That pattern powers retrieval-augmented generation, where a language model answers using relevant stored passages, as well as semantic search and recommendation systems.

The service is fully managed and serverless, so developers don’t provision servers or manage indexes by hand, and it scales with usage. It supports metadata filtering, hybrid search that combines keyword and semantic methods, namespaces to separate data, and tools for generating embeddings and reranking results. Pinecone also offers an assistant product that handles document chat with minimal setup, and integrations with LangChain, LlamaIndex, and the major model providers.

item.title: Poe
item.description:
Poe gives access to many AI models without separate accounts. A single app and website lets you switch between leading chatbots, image generators, and video tools, compare answers, and keep your conversations in one place. This is helpful for people who want to try different models and use whichever works best for each task.

Creators can build bots on top of models with custom prompts and knowledge, and publish them for others, with ways to earn revenue based on usage. The platform also offers an app builder and an API so developers can use Poe’s models in their projects. Group chats let multiple bots and people interact in one conversation.

item.title: Polycam
item.description:
Polycam makes 3D scanning accessible. A user walks around an object or room with their phone, the app captures images or LiDAR depth data, and processing creates a textured 3D model. Models can be measured, shared, and exported for use in design, games, or construction.

Modes include photo-based capture for detail, LiDAR for room scans and floor plans, and tools to build models from photos taken with any camera. Newer features include Gaussian splatting for realistic views and AI tools for generating models from images.

item.title: Railway
item.description:
Railway makes hosting feel easy. A developer connects a GitHub repository, and Railway detects the language, builds the app, and runs it, with databases like Postgres, Redis, and MySQL added in a click. Environments, variables, and networking are managed in a visual canvas.

Usage-based pricing and preview environments suit small teams, startups, and side projects. Many AI app builders and hobbyists use it to deploy back ends quickly. Features include cron jobs, volumes for storage, and private networking.

item.title: Raycast AI
item.description:
Raycast puts a command bar on your keyboard. Press a hotkey, type a few letters, and you can launch apps, search files, run calculations, manage windows, paste snippets, control music, and use hundreds of extensions that connect to tools such as GitHub, Linear, Notion, and Slack. Power users value how much it can cut mouse use and context switching.

Raycast AI adds chat and commands powered by leading language models. You can ask a question, rewrite selected text, summarize a page, translate, or run custom AI commands from any app, and switch among models from different providers. AI Extensions let the assistant act through extensions, such as creating an issue or checking a calendar, and Model Context Protocol support connects it to more tools. Chats and presets are synced across devices.

item.title: Real-ESRGAN
item.description:
Real-ESRGAN takes a small, blurry, or compressed image and produces a larger, cleaner version. It was trained on synthetic damage that imitates real-world degradation, such as blur, noise, and compression artifacts, so it handles messy sources better than older upscalers that assumed clean images. The results often look natural, with sharper edges and textures, although the model adds plausible detail instead of recovering what was truly there.

The project provides several models, including one for general photos and one for anime and illustrations, plus tools for video that process frames. Portable builds run on Windows, macOS, and Linux using Vulkan, so no complicated setup or Nvidia GPU is needed, and Python code lets developers integrate it. It is often paired with GFPGAN for face restoration. Many commercial upscaling tools and apps use Real-ESRGAN or models derived from it.

item.title: Recharge
item.description:
Recharge enables subscribe-and-save models for online stores. Merchants on Shopify and other platforms set up subscription products, let customers manage deliveries and payments in a portal, and bill on schedule. It is common in consumables such as food, supplements, and beauty products.

Analytics show retention, churn, and revenue, and tools help reduce cancellations. Smart payment retries recover failed charges, and AI models predict which subscribers may leave so merchants can intervene with offers or pauses.

item.title: Retool AI
item.description:
Retool is designed for engineers who need to build internal software quickly. Developers connect databases, APIs, and services, drag components such as tables, forms, and charts onto a canvas, and write queries and logic in SQL and JavaScript where needed. The result is an application for operations, support, or finance teams to manage data, approve requests, or run workflows, built in hours instead of weeks.

AI is integrated across the platform. A generative assistant can create an app from a description, write queries, and generate components, and Retool offers AI actions to classify, summarize, and extract information as parts of apps and workflows. Retool Agents let teams build agents that use their data and tools, and workflows automate scheduled and event-driven tasks. Enterprise controls cover permissions, audit logs, and self-hosting.

item.title: RunPod
item.description:
RunPod rents GPU computing in several forms. Users launch pods with a chosen GPU for development and training, or deploy serverless endpoints that scale with traffic for inference. Templates for common tools like Stable Diffusion and popular language model setups speed up starting.

Storage volumes persist data across sessions, and a community cloud offers lower prices on capacity from independent hosts alongside a secure cloud with data center hardware. Per-second billing suits bursty work.

item.title: Runway
item.description:
Runway builds tools for creative professionals. Its generative video models create clips from text or images, and a suite of editing tools handles tasks like removing backgrounds, changing motion, extending shots, and applying styles. Everything runs in the browser.

The company began with accessible video editing and became a leader in generative video, working with artists and studios. Newer models offer longer clips, better consistency, and controls for camera and motion, and the platform includes workflows for combining generation with traditional editing.

item.title: Runway
item.description: Runway is one of the original AI video companies, and it built its tools with filmmakers and artists in mind. The core of the product is its Gen video models, which create short clips from a text prompt, a still image, or both. Reference images help keep a character or setting consistent from one shot to the next, which is the hard part of making anything longer than a single clip. The company started as a set of browser-based editing tools, and some of that remains, such as background removal, motion tracking, and inpainting.

item.title: Runway Gen-3
item.description:
Gen-3 Alpha improved on earlier versions with finer detail, better handling of motion, and more consistent results across frames. Users could generate clips of several seconds from a prompt, an image, or both, with controls for camera movement and style.

It was trained on both images and video, aiming to understand how things move, and supported features such as image-to-video and video-to-video. Filmmakers and agencies used it for concept work, ads, and visual effects experiments.

item.title: SeaArt
item.description: SeaArt gives users a rich set of image generation tools in a friendly interface. You write a prompt, choose among many models and styles, and generate images, with options such as ControlNet to guide pose or composition and LoRA models to apply particular styles or characters. A library of community-shared models, workflows, and characters lets users build on others’ work, and a node-based workflow editor offers more advanced control for those who want it.

item.title: SketchUp
item.description: SketchUp is known for being easy to learn. Its core idea is pushing and pulling flat shapes into 3D forms, which makes it quick to sketch a building, a room, or a piece of furniture. Architects use it for early design, interior designers for layouts, and construction and woodworking professionals for planning and shop drawings. The 3D Warehouse offers a huge library of free models of furniture, fixtures, and building components.

item.title: SmolAgents
item.description: SmolAgents is designed to be easy to read and use. The core logic fits in a small amount of code, and building an agent takes a few lines: you pick a model, give it tools, and run a task. Its signature idea is the code agent, where the model writes its actions as Python code instead of structured tool calls. This lets it combine steps, use loops and variables, and handle multi-step problems efficiently, and the approach often needs fewer steps than traditional methods.

item.title: Sourcegraph Cody
item.description: Cody grew out of Sourcegraph’s code search, which indexes entire repositories and lets developers find and understand code across many projects. That context was its main advantage: instead of guessing from the open file, Cody could draw on the broader codebase to answer questions, write code that matched existing patterns, and explain how parts of a system fit together. It worked in VS Code, JetBrains IDEs, and the web, with chat, autocomplete, and commands to edit and test code.

item.title: Spline
item.description:
Spline brings 3D to web designers. In a browser editor that feels more like Figma than Blender, you create shapes, materials, lighting, and animations, then add interactions such as hover effects and clicks. Scenes can be published as links, embedded in websites, or exported to code, and they run in real time in the browser. It’s used for product landing pages, interactive hero sections, games, and design prototypes.

Collaboration and AI features set it apart from traditional 3D tools. Multiple people can edit a scene at once with comments and version history. AI tools can generate 3D objects and textures from text, help with animation, and create scenes from prompts. Physics, particles, and state-based interactions add depth, and integrations with Figma let designers bring in 2D elements.

item.title: Stable Video Diffusion
item.description:
Stable Video Diffusion extends the Stable Diffusion approach to motion. A user supplies a still image, and the model generates a few seconds of video that animates the scene. It was released with open weights, so researchers and hobbyists could run and adapt it.

Many later tools and workflows built on it, adding controls, longer clips, and fine-tunes. It helped prove that open video models were feasible, though newer models from other labs have surpassed it in length and quality.

item.title: Together AI
item.description:
Together AI hosts open models such as Llama, Qwen, and DeepSeek, and offers a developer-friendly API compatible with common formats. Its inference stack is tuned for speed, and options range from pay-per-token serverless access to dedicated endpoints for steady workloads.

Customization is a second focus. Teams can fine-tune models on their data, train at scale on GPU clusters, and run batch jobs at lower cost. The company’s research contributions in efficient attention and inference feed into its products.

item.title: Topaz Photo AI
item.description:
Topaz Photo AI aims to fix the technical flaws in photos with little effort. When you open an image, it analyzes the content and suggests corrections, using models for noise reduction, sharpening, and increasing resolution. It handles problems like grainy high-ISO shots, soft focus, and motion blur, and can enlarge photos while adding believable detail. Many wildlife, sports, and event photographers use it to rescue difficult images.

The tool also offers face recovery, light adjustment, color balance, and a way to apply different adjustments to selected subjects. It can be run as a standalone application, as an external editor from Lightroom, or as a plugin for Photoshop, and processes batches of images. Models run locally on your computer and benefit from a good graphics card.

item.title: Topaz Video AI
item.description:
Topaz Video AI improves footage after it has been shot. Its models upscale low-resolution video to HD or 4K, remove noise and compression artifacts, and sharpen soft footage. Frame interpolation creates additional frames to make slow motion smoother or convert a low frame rate to a higher one, and stabilization steadies shaky shots. Archivists restoring old film and videographers rescuing difficult footage use it often.

Different models are tuned for different problems, such as live action, animation, or low-quality sources. Newer diffusion-based models aim for higher-quality enhancement of detail, at the cost of heavy processing. The app lets you preview results on short clips before processing a whole video, supports batch processing and command-line use, and exports to common formats, with some cloud options for heavy models.

item.title: Turnitin
item.description:
Turnitin compares student submissions against a large database of papers, publications, and web content, producing a similarity report for instructors. It integrates with systems such as Canvas, Blackboard, and Moodle, so checking fits into grading.

An AI writing indicator estimates how much of a submission may be AI generated. AI detection is imperfect: false positives and negatives occur, and results are best used as a prompt for conversation, not proof. Feedback and grading tools add other functions.

item.title: Vast.ai
item.description:
Vast.ai connects people who need GPU compute with those who have spare capacity. Hosts, from individuals with gaming rigs to data centers, list machines with details and prices, and users search by GPU type, memory, location, and reliability, then launch containers on them. The competition among hosts keeps prices lower than on-demand rates from large cloud providers.

The platform provides tools for launching Docker-based environments, Jupyter notebooks, and templates for popular AI frameworks, and offers interruptible instances at deeper discounts as well as on-demand options. A range of GPUs is available, from consumer cards to data center models, which suits experimentation, rendering, fine-tuning, and inference for budget-conscious teams.

item.title: W&B Weave
item.description:
Weave addresses a common problem with LLM apps: it is hard to know what they are doing. Adding a few lines of code logs each call with its inputs, outputs, latency, cost, and the surrounding function calls, so a developer can inspect a failing response step by step instead of guessing. The traces cover nested calls, which matters for agents that chain several models and tools.

It also handles evaluation. Teams build datasets of test cases, define scorers (including LLM judges), and run experiments to compare prompts, models, and app versions before shipping. Results are tracked over time, which makes it easier to tell whether a change actually helped. Online evaluations can score live traffic and flag regressions in production.

item.title: Weather.ai
item.description:
Weather.ai positions itself as a forecast service built on machine learning rather than only traditional physics models. It aims to give hourly and daily forecasts for specific locations, which is the kind of hyperlocal output people want for planning a run, a trip, or an event. The site focuses on readable forecasts, and an API is available for developers.

Machine learning is now common in weather prediction. Large research efforts from Google DeepMind, NVIDIA, and others have shown that models trained on decades of observations can produce competitive forecasts quickly, and many startups sell tailored predictions built on this work. Services in this space usually combine public data from national weather agencies with their own models and corrections.

item.title: WeatherBug
item.description:
WeatherBug built its name on a dense network of weather stations, often at schools and other local sites. That gives it temperature, wind, and rain readings from places closer to you than a distant airport sensor, which helps when conditions change quickly, such as during a storm. The app combines that observation data with forecast models for hourly and multi-day outlooks.

Its mobile app is the main product. Users get radar maps, lightning detection, and alerts for severe weather and rainfall, along with air quality and pollen information in some regions. A subscription removes ads and unlocks extra features, and some of the forecasting uses machine learning to adjust model output for local conditions.

item.title: Zapier
item.description:
Zapier lets people automate work between apps without programming. A Zap starts with a trigger, such as a new form entry, and performs actions in other apps, like adding a row to a spreadsheet and sending a Slack message. It connects thousands of products.

AI has become part of the platform. Users describe an automation in plain language, add AI steps that summarize or classify data, and build agents that act across apps. Tables, forms, and interfaces let teams build small apps around their automations.

item.title: Zapier
item.description:
Zapier handles the plumbing between business apps. A workflow listens for an event in one tool and does something in another, with filters, paths, and delays to model real processes. Templates cover common needs in sales, marketing, and operations.

Newer capabilities include AI actions that read and write text, agents that carry out multi-step tasks, and an MCP offering that exposes Zapier actions to AI assistants. Teams can monitor runs, handle errors, and manage access centrally.

item.title: Zapier
item.description: Zapier connects the apps a business already uses and lets them pass data to each other without code. You build a Zap with a trigger, such as a new form submission, and one or more actions, such as adding a row to a spreadsheet, posting in Slack, and creating a CRM contact. It supports thousands of apps, from Gmail and Salesforce to niche tools, which is the main reason people choose it over building integrations by hand. Filters, paths, and delays let a Zap branch and wait, and a multi-step workflow can handle surprisingly complicated processes.

item.title: Zest AI
item.description:
Zest AI helps lenders approve more borrowers safely. Its models use many variables to estimate credit risk, aiming to include people thin credit files would exclude while keeping losses in check. Lenders deploy the models in their own decisioning workflows.

Explainability is central, since regulators require lenders to give reasons for adverse decisions. Zest provides tools to explain scores and to test models for disparate impact across groups. Credit unions and community banks are among its customers.

item.title: Zillow
item.description:
Zillow is where many people begin looking for a home. Listings for sale and rent appear on maps and lists with photos, price history, taxes, and school details, and users can filter by price, size, and features, save searches, and get alerts when matching homes appear. Agents and landlords pay to advertise or manage listings.

Its signature feature is the Zestimate, an automated estimate of a home’s value based on public records, market data, and a machine learning model. It is useful as a rough guide but can be off for individual homes, and sellers should not treat it as an appraisal. Zillow also offers mortgage and agent referral services, rental tools, and an AI-powered search that accepts natural language descriptions.

item.title: 01.AI
item.description:
01.AI started with the goal of building leading large language models. Its Yi series, released with open weights, performed strongly on benchmarks for its size and supported long context and Chinese and English. Developers around the world downloaded and fine-tuned the models, and the company also offered an API and consumer products. Kai-Fu Lee, a well-known AI executive and investor, led the company.

The company’s strategy changed as the cost of competing at the frontier rose and powerful open models from other Chinese labs became available. It reduced its investment in pretraining its own large models and moved toward selling AI solutions to businesses, using other models where appropriate. Reports describe a focus on enterprise data infrastructure and a path toward a public listing.

item.title: Alpha3D
item.description: Alpha3D addresses a bottleneck in 3D content: modeling each object by hand is slow and expensive. Instead, you upload a photo of a product or describe an object in text, and the platform generates a 3D model, typically within minutes. The models can be downloaded in common formats such as GLB for use in game engines, web viewers, and AR experiences. The company positions it for retail, gaming, and virtual try-on.

item.title: Botpress
item.description: Botpress started as an open-source tool for building chatbots with visual flows, and it grew into a platform around large language models. Developers and technical teams build agents that talk with customers on websites and messaging channels, connect to knowledge bases, and call APIs to do things like check an order or update an account. A visual builder and code options sit side by side, so non-engineers can adjust conversations while developers handle integrations.

item.title: Chroma
item.description:
Chroma is a vector database aimed at developer simplicity. It stores embeddings, which are numerical representations of text, images, or other data, along with metadata and the original documents. Applications query it to find items similar in meaning to a given input, which is the core of semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation.

It is easy to start: a few lines of Python or JavaScript create a collection, add documents, and run queries, and it can run in memory inside a program, as a local server, or in a hosted cloud service. It integrates with LangChain, LlamaIndex, and other frameworks, which made it a common choice for prototypes.

item.title: Cleanlab
item.description:
Cleanlab starts from the idea that model quality depends on data quality. Real datasets contain mistakes: images with wrong labels, duplicated examples, and outliers. Cleanlab’s open-source library uses statistical methods and model predictions to find the examples most likely to be wrong, so a team can correct them instead of reviewing everything.

The commercial platform, Cleanlab Studio, extends this with a no-code interface for cleaning and improving datasets and training models on the result. The company has also moved into reliability for generative AI, offering tools to score the trustworthiness of language model outputs and catch hallucinations in production systems.

item.title: Constructor
item.description:
Constructor serves online retailers that want search and discovery to drive revenue. Its engine powers site search, category pages, and recommendations, ranking products using both shopper behavior and business goals such as margin or inventory. Merchandisers can steer results with rules while the system learns from clicks and purchases.

Additional tools include product quizzes that guide shoppers to the right item, personalization that adapts to each visitor, and analytics that show how discovery affects sales. Generative AI features allow conversational shopping assistants that answer questions and suggest products.

item.title: Convai
item.description:
Convai makes game characters that respond to what players say. A developer defines a character’s personality, backstory, and knowledge, and Convai handles listening to speech, generating replies with a language model, speaking them with a synthetic voice, and driving lip sync and gestures. Plugins integrate with Unity, Unreal Engine, and other platforms.

Characters can also take actions in the game world, such as navigating or interacting with objects, based on conversation. Use cases include immersive games, training simulations, virtual tours, and educational experiences where open-ended dialogue adds value over scripted lines.

item.title: Diffbot
item.description:
Diffbot uses computer vision and natural language processing to read web pages the way a person would. Instead of writing a scraper for each site, developers send a URL to its APIs and receive structured data about articles, products, or people, regardless of page layout.

The company also built a large knowledge graph, a database of entities such as organizations, people, and products, with relationships collected from across the web. Customers query it to enrich records, monitor news, find companies matching criteria, or give language models grounded facts. Its extraction tools support crawling at scale.

item.title: Humanloop
item.description:
Humanloop helped teams build reliable applications on language models. Developers managed and versioned prompts, ran automated and human evaluations, and monitored behavior in production. It was used by enterprises that needed to test changes before shipping and keep a record of how prompts evolved.

Anthropic hired the company’s co-founders and most of its team, without acquiring the product or its intellectual property. The standalone service was wound down shortly afterward, and customers were given guidance for migrating to other tools.

item.title: Instabase
item.description:
Instabase focuses on complex documents that older template-based tools could not handle. Mortgage packages, insurance claims, and financial statements arrive in many formats, and Instabase uses AI models to classify them, extract data, and validate it against rules. Results flow into systems such as loan origination and claims platforms.

Its platform provides tools for building document workflows with a mix of models and human review, and newer products use language models for understanding and answering questions about documents. Customers can deploy it in the cloud or in their own environment, which matters for regulated data.

item.title: Iterable
item.description:
Iterable lets marketers build cross-channel journeys. They segment customers by behavior, design workflows in a visual canvas, and send messages triggered by actions, such as signing up, abandoning a cart, or reaching a milestone. Data from websites, apps, and warehouses feeds the profile used for personalization.

AI assists in several areas: optimizing the time a message is sent for each person, predicting engagement, recommending content, and helping generate copy. Experimentation tools test variants, and analytics tie campaigns to outcomes. Integration with data warehouses supports teams that centralize customer data.

item.title: Lakera
item.description:
Lakera defends applications built on language models. Its Guard product sits between users and a model, scanning prompts for attempts to override instructions, extract secrets, or inject malicious content, and checking outputs for leaks and harmful material. Developers add it with an API call.

The company grew out of research on adversarial attacks and became known for Gandalf, a public game where players try to trick a model into revealing a password, which generated a large dataset of attacks. Red teaming tools test applications before launch.

item.title: Langfuse
item.description:
Langfuse gives developers visibility into LLM applications. By adding its SDK or an integration, each request is traced with its prompts, model responses, tool calls, latency, and cost, including nested steps in agent workflows. Engineers inspect failures in a web interface and see usage across users and sessions.

Beyond observability, it supports quality work. Prompt management lets teams version and deploy prompts without code changes, evaluation features score outputs through LLM judges, user feedback, or custom checks, and datasets let teams run experiments before release. The product can be self-hosted, which suits privacy-sensitive teams.

item.title: LangSmith
item.description:
LangSmith helps teams understand and improve AI applications. Developers send traces from their applications, and LangSmith shows each step: prompts, retrieved documents, tool calls, and model outputs, with timing and cost. This makes it possible to find where an agent went wrong.

Evaluation is the second pillar. Teams build datasets from real traffic, run experiments across prompt or model versions, and score results with automated evaluators or human review. Monitoring dashboards and alerts track quality in production, and a deployment product hosts agents built with LangGraph.

item.title: Latitude
item.description:
Latitude makes interactive fiction with AI. Its best-known product, AI Dungeon, lets players describe any action in natural language, and an AI game master responds with the next part of the story. The result is open-ended storytelling that can go in any direction, from fantasy quests to comedy and mystery.

The studio has experimented with other AI-driven games and with platforms for creators who want to build their own AI-powered worlds. It uses a mix of language models, including models it trains and fine-tunes, and offers different tiers of models to subscribers.

item.title: Lexica
item.description:
Lexica began as a searchable archive of AI-generated images with the prompts that created them. Browsing the archive helped people learn how wording affects results, and copy ideas for their own generations. That made it a popular learning resource in the early days of image generators.

The platform added its own image generation models and an editor, so users can create images, refine them, and organize collections. It offers different model options and tools for art, product shots, and concepts. The community library remains a source of inspiration.

item.title: LiteLLM
item.description:
LiteLLM solves the problem of integrating many model providers. Developers write code once against the OpenAI format, and LiteLLM translates the call to the provider they choose. Switching models then means changing a name, not rewriting code.

The proxy server adds features for teams: a gateway with virtual keys, budgets and rate limits per team, logging, load balancing across deployments, and automatic fallback when a provider fails. Platform teams use it to give internal users a controlled path to models and to track costs.

item.title: Mastra
item.description:
Mastra targets JavaScript and TypeScript developers who build AI features. It provides building blocks: agents that call tools, workflows with steps and branching, retrieval over documents, memory, evaluations, and observability. Developers can run it locally with a playground to test and debug.

Its design fits the web stack, with deployment options for serverless platforms and integration with frameworks like Next.js. It works with models from many providers through a common interface and supports the Model Context Protocol. A hosted platform offers deployment and monitoring.

item.title: Mem0
item.description:
Mem0 gives AI applications a long-term memory. Language models forget everything between conversations unless the application supplies context. Mem0 extracts important facts from interactions, stores them, and retrieves the relevant ones when needed, so a chatbot can recall a user’s preferences or past requests.

Developers add it with a few API calls or a library, and it works with common models and frameworks. It supports user, session, and agent level memory, and a hosted platform manages storage and scaling. Use cases include personal assistants, customer support, and tutoring.

item.title: Neon
item.description:
Neon runs PostgreSQL in the cloud with a design that lets databases scale to zero when idle and start quickly when needed. Because storage and compute are separate, it can create copy-on-write branches of a database instantly, which suits testing, previews, and development workflows.

Branching has become useful for AI work, where agents and coding tools create databases on the fly. The pgvector extension supports embeddings and similarity search, so developers can store vectors next to ordinary data. The platform is used with frameworks like Next.js and with serverless hosts.

item.title: Nous Research
item.description:
Nous Research started as a group of researchers and hobbyists working in the open. Its Hermes models fine-tune open base models to follow instructions, use tools, and handle roleplay and reasoning, and have been popular among people running models locally. Data, methods, and weights are shared publicly.

The group has also worked on decentralized training, exploring ways to train large models across many machines run by different parties, and on tooling for agents. It operates as a company and offers access to its models through an API and an agent product.

item.title: PathAI
item.description:
PathAI works on digital pathology. Pathologists traditionally examine tissue slides under a microscope. With scanned slides, algorithms can highlight regions of interest, count cells, and measure biomarkers, which helps make reads more consistent. PathAI builds these tools and a platform for viewing and managing slides.

The company also supports pharmaceutical research. Its models analyze tissue from clinical trials to measure disease features and treatment responses, and it operates a laboratory service. The goal is to reduce variability and speed drug development.

item.title: Patronus AI
item.description:
Patronus AI helps teams find problems in AI applications. Developers run test sets through their systems, and Patronus scores the outputs with evaluators that check for hallucinations, unsafe content, leaks of sensitive data, and policy violations. Red-teaming tools probe for weaknesses with adversarial inputs.

The company has published benchmarks, including tests for financial question answering, and trained evaluation models such as a judge model for hallucination detection. Monitoring features watch production traffic and alert teams to drops in quality.

item.title: PearAI
item.description:
PearAI is a standalone editor forked from VS Code, with AI features built in. Developers get code completion, a chat panel that understands the project, and inline editing, and can connect their preferred models. Because it is a fork, familiar extensions and settings carry over.

It positions itself as an open alternative to Cursor and Windsurf. The AI layer builds on Continue, an open-source assistant. The project had a licensing controversy early on regarding its use of existing code, which it has since addressed.

item.title: PixAI
item.description:
PixAI is built around anime-style generation. Users type prompts, pick models trained for particular looks, and generate images. A feed of community creations offers inspiration, and sharing prompts lets others learn techniques.

Features include image-to-image transformation, model and LoRA libraries, and tools for creating characters consistently. A mobile app and credit system support casual use.

PixAI has a free tier with daily credits and paid plans. Community models can be trained on artwork without artists’ consent, which is controversial, and content rules apply to the platform. Alternatives include Civitai, Leonardo AI, NovelAI, Midjourney with niji, and Tensor.Art. PixAI suits anime fans and illustrators exploring AI art.

item.title: Poolside
item.description:
Poolside focuses on one domain: code. The company trains large models from scratch, using reinforcement learning where the model writes code, runs it, and learns from whether it works. The aim is models that handle real software tasks reliably.

It targets customers with strict security needs, such as defense and large enterprises, and offers deployment in their own environments. Products include a coding assistant and an agent built on its models, and the company has invested heavily in computing infrastructure.

item.title: Portkey
item.description:
Portkey sits between applications and model providers. Developers send requests to Portkey, which forwards them to the chosen provider and handles retries, fallbacks to other models, caching, and load balancing. This increases reliability and makes it easy to switch models.

The platform adds visibility and governance: logs and analytics on cost and latency, prompt management, guardrails that check inputs and outputs, and budgets and access controls for teams. It supports the Model Context Protocol and agent frameworks.

item.title: PromptLayer
item.description:
PromptLayer separates prompts from code. Teams store prompts in a registry, version them, test changes against datasets, and deploy new versions without redeploying the application. Non-engineers, such as product managers and domain experts, can edit prompts in a visual interface.

Observability features log every call with inputs, outputs, cost, and latency, and let teams search and analyze history. Evaluations compare prompt versions and models, and workflows chain steps for agents.

item.title: Ray
item.description:
Ray makes it easier to run Python code across many machines. A developer adds simple decorators to turn functions into distributed tasks, and Ray schedules them across a cluster. On top of this core sit libraries for data processing, training, tuning, and serving models.

It is widely used in machine learning: large model training jobs, batch inference, and reinforcement learning rely on it, and major AI labs and companies build on it. Anyscale, the company founded by its creators, offers a managed platform.

item.title: Rodin
item.description:
Rodin creates 3D assets from simple inputs. A user types a description or uploads an image, and the system produces a textured 3D model that can be exported to common formats. It also offers options for controlling geometry and materials.

The output can serve as a starting point for games, animation, product visualization, and augmented reality. Quality has improved quickly in this field, but generated meshes often need cleanup of topology and textures before production use.

item.title: Shortly AI
item.description:
Shortly AI was one of the early GPT-based writing tools built for fiction and long-form content. A writer types, and with a keystroke the assistant continues the text in the same voice, or offers rewrites and alternatives. It aimed to keep the writer in control of the direction.

It was used for blog posts, stories, and essays, particularly to push through slow stretches. The product emerged before general chat assistants became widely used, and those assistants now cover much of the same ground.

item.title: Sloyd
item.description:
Sloyd takes a different approach from mesh generators. Its models are parametric, so a user can generate a chair or a sword and then adjust sliders for size, shape, and style, and get clean, game-ready geometry with proper topology. Real-time generation fits into workflows and game engines.

A library of templates and an API let developers generate assets inside their own tools and games, including at runtime. The aim is to reduce the time artists spend on common props and set dressing.

item.title: Tavily
item.description:
Tavily provides web search for machines. A developer sends a query and receives ranked results with cleaned content and sources, trimmed to what a language model needs, so agents can ground answers in current information. Extra endpoints extract text from pages, crawl sites, and run deeper research.

It integrates with frameworks like LangChain and LlamaIndex and with the Model Context Protocol, which made it a common choice for adding web access to agents. A free tier supports experimentation.

item.title: Vellum
item.description:
