Vellum supports teams building AI features for production. Developers and product managers write and compare prompts across models, build workflows that chain steps, and run evaluations against test sets before releasing changes.

Deployment and monitoring tools track versions, costs, and quality, and let teams update prompts without redeploying code. A visual builder and SDK suit both technical and non-technical members.

Vellum has a free tier and paid plans. Alternatives include Langfuse, LangSmith, Braintrust, PromptLayer, and Humanloop, which has shut down. Vellum suits product teams shipping LLM features.

item.title: Vic.ai
item.description:
Vic.ai reads invoices and processes them with little manual input. It extracts data, suggests coding to the correct accounts, routes approvals, and flags unusual items, learning from how accountants correct it. The aim is touchless processing for routine invoices.

It integrates with ERP systems such as NetSuite, SAP, and Microsoft Dynamics, and offers payment and analytics features. Accounting firms and mid-sized to large finance teams use it to cut manual work.

item.title: AI Aware
item.description:
AI Aware presents itself as a tool for checking whether content was written or generated by AI. Users upload a document or paste text, and the service returns an estimate of how likely it is to be machine-generated, along with detail on which parts raised the score. The idea is to give educators, publishers, and businesses a quick way to screen material.

Detection of AI-generated content is a difficult problem. Detectors rely on statistical patterns that can also appear in human writing, especially in formal or non-native text, and they can be fooled by editing or paraphrasing. For that reason, any score should be treated as a hint that calls for further review rather than as proof.

item.title: Anna
item.description:
Anna presents itself as an adaptive AI companion. Instead of treating every chat as new, it tries to remember what you have told it and adjusts its tone and suggestions as it learns your preferences and goals. That continuity is the main selling point of companion-style apps.

People use apps like this for conversation, motivation, planning, and reflection. They differ from task-focused assistants in that they emphasize an ongoing relationship. Mainstream assistants such as ChatGPT and Claude have also added memory, so the line between categories is blurring.

item.title: Character.ai
item.description: Character.AI lets you chat with an enormous catalog of AI personalities. Some are based on fictional characters or historical figures, many are invented by users, and you can build your own by writing a description of who the character is and how they talk. The results feel more like acting than answering questions: the characters stay in persona, remember what you have said in the conversation, and respond in a distinctive voice. Users spend long sessions on it, using it for role-play, story writing, language practice, and casual company.

item.title: ChatPlayground AI
item.description:
ChatPlayground addresses a simple question: which model is best for this task? Instead of opening several chatbots in separate tabs, a user types a prompt once and sees answers from multiple models side by side, including offerings from OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, DeepSeek, and open models.

That helps with writing, coding, and research tasks where quality varies by model. Users can save conversations, keep prompts organized, and switch between models while working. For people who pay for several subscriptions, a single place can be convenient.

item.title: Cline
item.description: Cline is an autonomous coding assistant that lives in your editor. You describe a task, and it works through it: reading the relevant files, proposing edits, running commands, and checking the result. It has a Plan mode, where it explores the project and agrees an approach with you, and an Act mode, where it carries the plan out. Each file change and terminal command is shown for your approval, so you stay in control, though you can switch on auto-approval for lower-risk actions.

item.title: DALL-E 3
item.description:
DALL-E 3 was a text-to-image model known for following detailed prompts closely. Its integration with ChatGPT let users describe an image in conversation and have the assistant refine the prompt, which made image generation accessible to people who had never used a dedicated art tool. Developers could also call it through OpenAI’s API.

It was part of a line that began with the original DALL-E and DALL-E 2, which helped popularize text-to-image generation. Over time, OpenAI moved to newer image models built natively into its multimodal systems, which handle text in images and edits better. DALL-E branding faded as a result.

item.title: Deepgram
item.description:
Deepgram sells speech AI to developers. Its speech-to-text API transcribes audio in real time or from recordings, and it is designed for accuracy at low latency and low cost, which matters for call centers, meeting tools, and voice assistants that process large volumes. Features include speaker labeling, punctuation, keyword boosting, and support for many languages, and models can be customized to a company’s vocabulary.

The platform has widened to cover the whole voice stack. A text-to-speech product generates natural voices with low latency, and a voice agent API combines speech recognition, a language model, and speech synthesis into a single service for building conversational agents that can hold phone calls. Enterprises can run Deepgram in their own cloud or on-premises when data cannot leave their control.

item.title: Grok
item.description: Grok is the chatbot from xAI, Elon Musk’s AI company. It is built into X, so you can ask it about a post, a trending topic, or a thread without leaving the feed, and it is also available as a separate app and at grok.com. Its main distinguishing feature is live access to posts on X, which makes it unusually quick at summarizing what people are saying about a breaking story. The tone is a little looser than other assistants, and it will answer some questions that more cautious tools decline.

item.title: Hailuo AI
item.description:
Hailuo AI is the consumer face of video models from MiniMax, a Chinese AI company. You type a prompt or upload an image, and it generates a short video clip, with motion that many users find natural, including complex movement like dancing, sports, and camera moves. It gained a following among creators for the quality of its image-to-video results and its willingness to follow detailed prompts.

The platform offers tools for steering results. A subject reference feature keeps a character consistent across clips, camera controls guide movement, and different model versions trade speed for quality. It also generates images and offers voice and music features through MiniMax’s other models. An API lets developers use the video models in their own products.

item.title: Luma Dream Machine
item.description: Dream Machine is how most people first used Luma AI’s video models. You describe a scene or upload a still image, and it produces a short clip with motion, lighting, and camera movement that tends to look cinematic. Luma started as a 3D capture company, which still shows in how well its video models handle depth and camera moves. People use it for concept videos, storyboards, social content, product shots, and b-roll when a shoot is not practical.

item.title: Meshy
item.description:
Meshy makes 3D asset creation fast. You type a description or upload an image, and it generates a 3D mesh with textures in a minute or two. The results can be rotated, refined, and downloaded in common formats. Indie game developers, 3D printing hobbyists, product designers, and virtual world builders use it to produce props, characters, and environment pieces without modeling each from scratch.

The platform includes tools for the steps after generation. It can retexture a model from a prompt, remesh to adjust polygon counts and topology, and add skeletons and animations to characters. Plugins and an API connect it with Blender, Unity, Unreal Engine, Maya, and other tools, so assets can flow into existing pipelines. A library of community models provides starting points.

item.title: MySpec
item.description:
MySpec starts with the plan instead of the code. A user describes a product or feature, and the platform produces a specification covering requirements, architecture, and tasks. That document guides the build, whether a human or an AI coding agent does the work.

The idea responds to a common problem: coding agents given vague prompts produce inconsistent results. A clear spec gives the agent a target and gives the team something to review before time is spent. It fits the approach seen in tools like Kiro and GitHub’s Spec Kit.

item.title: NightCafe Studio
item.description:
NightCafe was one of the earliest AI art communities. It gives users access to various models, including Stable Diffusion variants, other leading generators, and its own options, so you can try different styles without separate accounts. You type a prompt, pick a model and style, and get images in seconds, then use tools to upscale, inpaint, or generate variations.

Community is a key part of the product. Users publish their creations, follow each other, join themed challenges, and vote, and a credit system rewards participation with free credits. Features like model training, text-to-video, and image-to-image extend what you can do, and prints on posters and canvases let people turn art into physical products. It is popular with hobbyists and casual creators.

item.title: Obsidian AI
item.description:
Obsidian’s approach to AI follows its general philosophy: keep the core simple and let users choose add-ons. Because notes are plain files in a folder, they work well with language models. Community plugins let you chat with your vault, ask questions about your notes, summarize long documents, rewrite text, and find related notes by meaning instead of keywords. Smart Connections and Copilot-style plugins are popular examples.

Users have a lot of freedom over where the AI runs. A plugin can send text to a hosted model like those from OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google using your own API key, or it can connect to a local model through tools such as Ollama or LM Studio, so notes never leave your computer. Some people also expose their vault to coding agents and assistants through the Model Context Protocol, which lets tools like Claude read and organize notes.

item.title: Obviously AI
item.description:
Obviously AI was built to make machine learning accessible to business users. You upload a CSV or connect a data source, choose the thing you want to predict, such as customer churn, sales, or lead conversion, and the platform tests multiple algorithms, picks the best one, and shows the results in plain language. It highlights which columns most influence the prediction and lets you try what-if scenarios.

Predictions can be exported or sent to other tools, and the platform offers dashboards for sharing insights with teammates. It positions itself for marketing, sales, finance, and operations analysts who have data but no data scientists, and for consultants who need quick models for clients.

item.title: Outfit.fm
item.description:
Outfit.fm addresses the cost of fashion photography. A seller photographs a garment on a hanger or flat, uploads it, and the tool generates images of the item on virtual models in settings that suit the brand. Options include different body types, poses, and backgrounds.

Small brands and online sellers use it to fill catalogs and social feeds without booking models, studios, and photographers. Speed lets them test styles and update visuals frequently.

item.title: PlayHT
item.description: PlayHT offered realistic text-to-speech with a large catalog of voices across many languages, plus voice cloning from short audio samples. Creators used its web studio to narrate videos, podcasts, and audiobooks, and developers used its API to add speech to apps and phone systems. Its later conversational models were built to sound natural in dialogue, with emotion and pacing, and the company also developed voice agents under the PlayAI name.

item.title: PrompTessor
item.description:
PrompTessor gives prompt writers a place to work. Users draft a prompt, get suggestions to improve its structure and clarity, run it against several models, and compare outputs. Analysis tools point out ambiguity and missing context.

Typical users are people who build assistants and automations and need consistent behavior, as well as individuals who want better results from chatbots. Saving and versioning prompts helps teams reuse what works.

Independent information is limited. As models get better at understanding short requests, built-in prompt improvers in chat apps cover some needs. PrompTessor has a free tier and paid plans. Alternatives include PromptPerfect, PromptLayer, Promptfoo, LangSmith playground, and Anthropic’s prompt tools. PrompTessor suits users who iterate on prompts.

item.title: Serno
item.description:
Serno gives users a single place to consult multiple models. A person asks a question once and sees how different systems respond, with differences highlighted, which can reveal uncertainty or disagreement that a single answer would hide.

This approach suits research, strategy, and decisions where one model’s blind spot could mislead. Saved conversations and comparisons make it easy to revisit reasoning, and some workflows ask models to critique each other.

item.title: The Influencer AI
item.description:
The Influencer AI generates a virtual person who can appear in ads, product demos, and social posts. A brand creates or selects a character and the tool produces images and videos of that character holding products, talking to the camera, or appearing in scenes, with consistent looks across content.

The pitch is cost and speed. Producing varied creative with real models requires scheduling, travel, and fees, while AI can generate many variations quickly for testing ads. Features include scripts, voices, and lip-synced video.

item.title: TheLibrarian.io
item.description:
TheLibrarian.io puts an assistant in WhatsApp. Users message it to check their email, schedule events, create tasks, and get reminders, in natural language or voice notes. It connects to services like Gmail and Google Calendar.

The appeal is simplicity: no new interface, and the chat is available anywhere. Connecting an assistant to email and calendars requires trust, so review permissions and privacy terms.

Independent information is limited. It has a free tier and paid plans. Alternatives include Notis, Poke, Lindy, Motion, and ChatGPT with connectors. TheLibrarian.io suits people who want to manage tasks through WhatsApp.

item.title: Wan Video
item.description:
Wan generates video from descriptions. Users provide a prompt or an image, and the model produces a clip with motion and detail. Alibaba has released several versions, including open-weight models that run on local hardware and have attracted a large community of tools and fine-tunes.

Creators and filmmakers use Wan for text-to-video, image-to-video, and editing tasks, through hosted sites and through open-source workflows such as ComfyUI. Open availability makes it a base for research and custom pipelines.

item.title: ZeroTwo
item.description:
ZeroTwo is a multi-model chat workspace. A user picks a model for each conversation or compares several, and keeps history, files, and prompts in one place. It supports web search, image generation, and document analysis.

For people who use several AI products, a combined interface can simplify life and cost. Pricing is typically a single subscription instead of many.

Access to the newest features of each provider may lag the official apps. ZeroTwo has a free tier and paid plans. Alternatives include Poe, TypingMind, ChatHub, OpenRouter’s chat, and Open WebUI. ZeroTwo suits power users who work across models.
